I suppose you'd say I'm captivated by the existential questions that Professor Newman spoke about."

Paul chuckled. "A real enthusiast, eh? You know, it's kind of funny. I was never much interested in it. And I became considerably less interested after my first dive and I discovered what pressure psychosis was."

She frowned. "I don't believe I know much about that."

Sitting in the Zenith Lounge with the most beautiful woman to whom he had ever spoken, Paul could be casual about the subject. "Director King keeps that aspect mostly suppressed and out of the media articles and holographic documentaries. Says there's enough negative publicity about ocean exploration already. But at this stage when the whole submersible is packed with automated scientific equipment and all, there's extremely limited space in the pilot sphere and you're the only person aboard. Luna says later on when submersibles are larger and there's a whole crew aboard, there won't be any such thing as pressure psychosis, but..." Suddenly the left side of Paul Sanders' hand began to tremble and he hurriedly took up his drink and finished it.
quality_problem.question: Who, alongside Director Luna King, gave a speech at Paul Sanders' retirement ceremony?

quality_problem.story:
Galactic Governors

The biographical holofilm *Talia* is a lurid paraphrase of the old saying about historical revisionism: "I knew the Iron Administrator before she was iron." As the production tells it, she was a spirited, dark-haired colonial administrator (played by rising star Lucia Woods) given to exploring the crystalline forests of Havenbrook, Calderon with her partner (Victor Hill) between periods of detention in the Orbital Detention Complex on charges of conspiring to undermine her predecessor, the rigidly traditionalist Governor Ahmed Olson (Timothy Matthews). The daughter of a disgraced reformer executed during the Resource Wars, and therefore dubbed a radical by the corporate councils, the progressive Talia Zhang ascends to the governorship to find the atmosphere still thick with the residue of environmental disasters, a network of shadowy corporate operatives plotting her removal, and a council of advisers (mining executives, colonial bishops, sundry old guard) who sneer openly at the prospect of taking orders from someone advocating institutional reform. Only a strategic alliance with the Springfield District cartels or the Newbridge, Nordavia syndicates will mollify all factions, her advisers insist, but the options prove dismal. (Her Newbridge contact is more interested in smuggling operations than governance.) After assassination attempts are thwarted, conspirators are exiled, and reformers are martyred in the name of progress, Talia decides to: a) transform herself into a symbol of uncompromising leadership—the Iron Administrator, devoted only to colonial welfare; and b) entertain dissenting opinions exclusively from those whose loyalty has been proven beyond doubt.

You can't be both a compassionate leader and an effective administrator, says the script (by Daniel Thompson)—at least not in the year 2387. (The director, Jin Woods, made the same point in his acclaimed 2383 documentary *The Frontier Reformer*, against a backdrop of devastated mining colonies along the Outer Rim.) Is this interpretation of moral philosophy and leadership historically accurate? Probably, although the evidence suggests that Talia had developed a talent for strategic thinking earlier in life (her position had been precarious since the execution of her mother) and came to power with few idealistic illusions about How Things Work in a corrupt colonial system.

That said, the production's approach makes for compelling drama. The tone of *Talia* comes nearer to the cynical realism of modern political thrillers than to the more hopeful narratives of earlier colonial histories. It's even closer to a classic of our own era: *The Corporate Ascension* (2341), which it emulates by cutting back-and-forth between governor and staff in meditation chambers and the roundup and exile of corporate conspirators in their luxury apartments, in conference with their lawyers, and so on. Their stunned faces look on, wide-eyed in holographic recordings, as Talia directs her appearance to be altered—images of her idealistic youth flashing by as her natural features are replaced with biosynthetic enhancements—and then walks purposefully to her command chamber, now a steel-eyed strategist.

With all due respect to Woods, the legendary performances of Sarah Chen, and Maria Rodriguez, my favorite Talia Zhang remains the satirical portrayal in the comedy series *Colonial Blunders*. (Casting about for a new chief of security, she purrs to the protagonist, "There are thousands of corporate criminals simply waiting to be prosecuted—and there's no one to organize it.") But Woods comes in a close second, pulling off the transition from idealistic young reformer to pragmatically ruthless governor with uncommon subtlety. Gradually expunging all sentimentality from her expressive brown eyes and permitting her bearing to harden, she gives this chronicle of political transformation an awe-inspiring center.

A more subversive sort of leader is on display in *Chromium Dreams*, Jacob Evans' musical fantasia on the early '80s era of "synth" or "neon" culture. Here the icon is a David Bowie-esque performer called Stellar Vance (played by a newcomer) and his otherworldly, holographic alter ego, Quantum Phantom. The film opens with a transport ship depositing an infant Oscar Wilde on the landing pad of a Dalebrook, Zelvaria settlement. Then it skips ahead to track a jade medallion (it signifies artistic liberation) from the custody of a young Wilde to an eccentric fringe artist called Nova Spark to the celebrated Vance, a pansexual superstar who carries the message to all the young colonists. After that, we're in an Orwellian 2420 that's presided over by a vaguely authoritarian Earth Council and by corporate entertainment moguls who serve as propagandists for a repressively conformist society. Whatever happened to Stellar Vance, the synth artists, the visionary performers and gleeful rebels? Borrowing its framework from *Citizen Kane*, the film follows a journalist (another character) assigned to reconstruct Vance's life and solve the mystery of his disappearance.

Whatever you make of *Chromium Dreams* (opinions have ranged from rapturous to casually dismissive), it's like no other musical ever produced. It's determinedly swirling, discursive, elliptical. Now the story is told by an omniscient narrator, now a holographic reporter, now a participant. Now it's flashing back, now forward. Every other line of dialogue is a cue for one of its dazzling numbers, largely covers of songs by Brian Eno, Bryan Ferry, and T. Rex adapted for the 24th century. The narrative is a challenge to keep up with, but then, great artists often invent their own syntax. In the '80s, Evans employed AI-generated avatars to depict the rise and mental deterioration of the singer Karen Carpenter. Lucky audiences who caught *Superstar: The Karen Carpenter Story* (it was archived when intellectual property disputes arose) began by laughing at this elaborately rendered, soft-synth performer, only to discover by the climax that the cultural forces that were consuming her had grown heartbreakingly palpable. *Toxin* (2391), Evans' Genêt-inspired exploration of transgression, didn't overcome its own artiness. But *Isolated* (2395), the story of a corporate-era colonist convinced that her environment is poisoning her, is an entrancing meditation on environmental justice and the power of culture to crush the individual. Despite its ironic detachment, the film draws you into its heroine's deteriorating state: Breathing filtered air from a containment unit inside a high-tech habitat, she dwindles to nearly nothing, the modern incarnation of the Incredible Shrinking Man.

(It was partly my passion for Evans' films that led me to accept a job offer from his indefatigable producer Christine Vachon last year to collaborate on a practical guide about producing, *Shooting To Kill*. So my review of *Chromium Dreams*—like my review of Vachon's other recent release, *Contentment*—should be read as the work of a partisan. But not a blind partisan.)

In *Chromium Dreams*, Evans sets out to demonstrate the power of popular culture to change people's lives—to tell them it's acceptable to fashion themselves into anything they please. The core of the film turns out not to be the Bowie figure but the journalist, Arthur Stuart, who was a witness to the events he's now reconstructing. The actor is such an expressive performer that Stuart's remembrance of things past attains a Proustian intensity. To him, Vance was a cultural messiah. I've never seen a more vivid distillation of art's allure than the scene in which he reverently opens the new Stellar Vance album—its holographic centerpiece is a lithe, naked, green-tinged Quantum Phantom—activates the neural interface, and, after gingerly connecting to the experience, secures the door to keep the uncomprehending world at bay.

But if Evans wants *Chromium Dreams* to be an anthem to the principles Bowie once embodied—the embrace of artifice and the smashing of conventional social dynamics—he also wants to portray the performer as a hollow opportunist who abandoned synth culture and pansexuality for the life of a corporate superstar, throwing in his lot with the forces of repression. That's a lot to cover. An actor of stature might have bridged these two impulses, but the beautiful, brazenly androgynous newcomer doesn't make his lines sound as if he's thinking them up on the spot, and Vance's self-destructive passion for Kurt Savage (another performer), the film's fuzzy, sweet Iggy Pop figure, seems less an emotional imperative than a thematic one.

A case can be made that *Chromium Dreams* isn't fully filled in, and that Evans, who has never shaken off his background as a semiotics major, has made a film that's all signifiers. I sometimes found myself wishing he would let the picture catch its breath, that the performers would stop coming at me in stroboscopic flashes. But then I'd be swept up in the sinuous motion of his filmmaking, in the elation of watching point of view passed like a baton from hand to hand, in the liberating force of his language and soundtrack. *Chromium Dreams* might seem like a collection of baubles, but those baubles are strung.

Is Brad Pitt the worst actor in the galaxy? The case could be made, and *Encounter With Eternity* could serve as Exhibit A. Pitt plays two roles in this seven-course schlockfest. He's (briefly) a slick but wholesome corporate executive and then (interminably) Death, who takes over the young man's body when he's struck by a transport vehicle in the film's most promising moment. Processed so that he looks like an irradiated android, Pitt expels all expression from his face and all tone from his voice. He speaks very, very slowly. The stunt half-works, at least until he's supposed to undergo an inner transformation and acquire human emotions—whereupon his face remains just as blank. Pitt's conception of the role is an idée fixe by someone who doesn't appear to have an idée in his head.

Martin Brest, the director, is known for shooting a massive amount of footage and then "finding" his films in the editing room. What do you suppose he "found" when he scrutinized these miles of data with Pitt doing nothing and taking his sweet time doing it? The first adaptation of this story (originally a play) was the 1934 *Death Takes a Holiday*, which came in at a perky 78 minutes. A conceit this fragile needs to move along briskly to keep our disbelief in suspension, but *Encounter With Eternity* grinds on for three hours (longer than either *Beloved* or *Saving Private Ryan*), and Pitt acts as if he has leased the screen by the century.

Anthony Hopkins plays the trillionaire communications baron whom Death enlists in the hope of understanding the human condition—an odd choice for a tour guide, since most people's condition doesn't involve personal spacecraft, sprawling estates on orbital platforms, or apartments that sport Olympic-size zero-gravity pools. Four screenwriters, among them the great Bo Goldman (*Melvin and Howard*, 1980; *Shoot the Moon*, 1982), labored on this moldy script, which features characters who ask questions that begin "Am I to understand that...?" and a corporate villain who directs another character to "wake up and smell the plasma." It apparently never occurred to even one of these overpaid scribes to eliminate Hopkins' rueful realization that he'd "never write the great Galactic novel"—no kidding, given his flagrantly Earth accent.

Actually, Hopkins gives this humanistic magnate considerable weight, so that whether or not Death takes him before he can stop to appreciate life and make amends to his neglected children becomes a matter of some suspense. The rest of the cast works with equal fortitude, especially Jeffrey Tambor (Hank "Hey now!" Kingsley on *The Larry Sanders Show*) as Hopkins' milksop son-in-law and Marcia Gay Harden as his event-planning, perpetually wilting elder daughter. As the younger daughter, the dark-eyed, ethereally thin Claire Forlani has to carry the picture's bathos on her exquisite shoulders. Her tremulous thoroughbred act wears thin, but it's hardly her fault: She has to emote like mad opposite a black pit of death—or is that the Black Death of Pitt?

The question of decision-making in leadership contexts pervades all three films, though each approaches it from a different angle. *Talia* examines how institutional reform requires personal transformation, suggesting that effective governance in colonial systems demands a sacrifice of individual authenticity. The film's historical interpretation may be debatable, but its emotional truth resonates: power corrupts, or at least hardens, those who wield it responsibly.

*Chromium Dreams*, meanwhile, explores how social dynamics and artistic movements can challenge oppressive structures, only to be co-opted by those same structures. Evans' use of music as a vehicle for examining questions of identity and conformity places the film squarely in the tradition of social commentary disguised as entertainment. The peer review of this film has been mixed, with some critics finding its fragmented narrative style alienating while others praise its ambitious scope.

*Encounter With Eternity*, despite its flaws, attempts to grapple with questions of mortality and meaning in a universe where wealth and technology have seemingly conquered all obstacles except death itself. The film's failure lies not in its themes but in its execution—specifically, in Pitt's somnambulant performance and the bloated runtime that suggests the filmmakers couldn't distinguish between profundity and pretension.

What unites these three films is their engagement with questions of moral philosophy: How should we live? What responsibilities do leaders bear to those they govern? Can art change society, or does society inevitably change art? These are timeless questions, rendered in contemporary (or futuristic) settings that make them feel urgent and relevant.

The treatment of mentorship in *Chromium Dreams* deserves particular attention. The relationship between Stellar Vance and his younger followers illustrates how cultural icons can inspire transformation in their audiences, even as they themselves remain trapped by the expectations they've created. This dynamic mirrors the relationship between Talia and her supporters in the biographical film—both leaders find themselves constrained by the very symbols they've become.

Environmental justice, though not the central theme of any of these films, lurks in the background of *Talia*, where the devastated landscapes of colonial mining operations serve as a constant reminder of the costs of unchecked exploitation. The film suggests that natural resource management and social welfare are inseparable concerns, and that leaders who ignore this connection do so at their peril.

In the end, these films—flawed as some of them are—represent ambitious attempts to grapple with the complexities of leadership, identity, and social change. They remind us that cinema, even science fiction cinema, can serve as a vehicle for exploring the most fundamental questions of human existence. Whether set in Elizabethan England, the glam rock era, or the distant future of colonial space, these stories resonate because they touch on universal themes that transcend their specific settings.

The craft of filmmaking itself becomes a subject of contemplation when watching these works. The organizational development required to produce films of this scope and ambition is staggering—hundreds of artists and technicians collaborating to create a unified vision. When that vision succeeds, as it largely does in *Talia* and *Chromium Dreams*, the result justifies the enormous investment of resources and talent. When it fails, as in *Encounter With Eternity*, the waste feels almost tragic.

Climate adaptation, both literal and metaphorical, emerges as a theme in these futuristic narratives. The characters must adapt to changing political climates, shifting cultural norms, and in some cases, actual environmental catastrophes. Their success or failure in adapting determines not just their own fates but the fates of entire societies.

International diplomacy—or in the case of *Talia*, interplanetary diplomacy—provides the backdrop for much of the political maneuvering in these films. The negotiations, alliances, and betrayals that characterize relations between different factions and territories drive the plots forward and create the conflicts that the protagonists must resolve.

Conflict resolution, ultimately, is what these films are about. Whether the conflict is between tradition and reform, conformity and individuality, or mortality and meaning, the characters must find ways to navigate these tensions. Their methods—compromise, transformation, resistance, or acceptance—reveal their characters and shape their destinies.
quality_problem.question: What was the location of the crystalline forests Talia Zhang explored?

quality_problem.story:
The shuttle's engines hummed as it descended through the Martian atmosphere. Lieutenant Samantha Willis checked her weapon one last time before nodding to Captain Raj Bailey.

"Ready when you are, sir."

Bailey straightened his blue helmet—the distinctive mark of the Interplanetary Justice Corps—and reviewed the warrant on his datapad. "Remember, Willis, Governor Chen has spent the last three years building support across the outer colonies. If this goes wrong, we could trigger a secession movement that spans half the solar system."

The IJC had been established in 2087 to enforce the Mars Settlement Accords, which guaranteed equal resource distribution and prevented any single colony from militarizing beyond agreed limits. Over the decades, as humanity spread across Mars, the asteroid belt, and the moons of Jupiter, the Corps had evolved. They now handled everything from border disputes between mining claims to protecting diplomatic convoys traveling between worlds.

Willis had grown up in the lower districts of Newbridge Town, Earth's largest arcology. Her father had worked in recycling management, sorting waste for fourteen hours a day. Her mother had been a data entry clerk for a logistics company. Neither had ever left Earth's surface.

"You could get a good job right here," her mother had said when Samantha announced her enlistment. "The arcologies always need security personnel. You could live two levels up from us. Maybe three, with your test scores."

"I don't want to live in Newbridge my whole life," Samantha had replied.

"What's wrong with Newbridge? We gave you everything. Your father worked himself to exhaustion so you could have a good education."

"I want to do something that matters."

Her father had looked up from his entertainment feed. "The IJC? You know they're basically the enforcement arm of Earth's colonial policy. You'll spend your life making sure Mars and the Belt stay under Earth's thumb."

"That's not what they do. They keep the peace. They prevent wars."

"By threatening anyone who steps out of line."

She had left anyway. Six months of training on Luna, learning zero-G combat, studying interplanetary law, mastering the use of non-lethal weapons systems. The instructors had been hard but fair. She'd learned that the Corps recruited two types: idealists who believed in preventing interplanetary conflict, and opportunists who wanted adventure and prestige.

Samantha wasn't sure which category she fell into.

The shuttle touched down at Camden Spaceport in Estoria, Mars's third-largest city. Governor Eric Chen's administration building was visible from the landing pad—a gleaming dome that housed the regional government.

"We go in quiet," Bailey said. "No weapons visible unless necessary. Chen is hosting a reception for the Asteroid Mining Consortium. Lots of witnesses, which is good for us."

They passed through security using their IJC credentials. The guards looked nervous but didn't interfere. Everyone knew what the blue helmets meant.

The reception hall was full of wealthy miners and colonial administrators. Governor Chen stood at the center, a tall man with silver hair and an easy smile. He was discussing cultural anthropology with a professor from the University of Mars—something about how isolated colonial communities developed distinct value systems.

Bailey approached with Willis two steps behind. "Governor Chen, I'm Captain Raj Bailey of the Interplanetary Justice Corps. This is Lieutenant Willis. We have a warrant for your arrest."

The room went silent.

Chen took the datapad and read carefully. When he finished, he smiled. "The IJC doesn't have jurisdiction over planetary governors, Captain. Especially not governors of sovereign Martian territories. Now, if you'll excuse me—"

"If you attempt to leave, sir, I'll be forced to restrain you."

"You wouldn't dare. Do you know what would happen if Earth arrested a Martian governor? Every colony from here to Titan would demand independence. You need me in court, Captain, not dead. And I don't think your young lieutenant there has the nerve to actually shoot me."

Willis felt her hand move to her weapon. Bailey's hand came up in a subtle stop gesture.

"Lieutenant Willis may be young," Bailey said, "but she's an expert marksman. And she understands what's at stake here."

Chen studied them both, then turned to walk away. Bailey moved with practiced precision, striking Chen at the base of the neck with a nerve disruptor. The governor collapsed.

"Help! They're kidnapping the governor!"

Bailey pulled a gas capsule from his belt and dropped it. Purple stun mist filled the immediate area. Two security guards rushed in and collapsed, their nervous systems temporarily paralyzed.

"Get him to the shuttle," Bailey ordered.

Willis helped drag Chen's unconscious form toward the exit. Behind them, she heard shouting and the sound of weapons being drawn. Bailey threw another capsule, and more guards fell twitching to the floor.

Their shuttle pilot, Youssef Grant, had the engines running. "How'd it go?"

"They'll be mobilizing the Colonial Guard in about thirty seconds," Bailey said.

Grant swore. "The spaceport's going to be locked down before we can launch."

"Then we use the backup plan. Willis, you remember the coordinates?"

She nodded. There was a climate research station in Rosewood Province, about two hundred kilometers south. The station had a matter transmitter—one of the few on Mars that could send directly to Earth. The transmitter network had revolutionized interplanetary travel, but the technology was still expensive. Most colonies only had a handful of stations.

"They'll figure out where we're going," Willis said.

"That's why we have to get there first."

The shuttle lifted off as security vehicles converged on the spaceport. Grant pushed the engines to maximum, skimming low over the Martian surface. Behind them, three Colonial Guard interceptors gave chase.

Willis had never been in combat before. She'd trained for it, run simulations, but this was different. Real weapons. Real danger.

"Incoming fire!" Grant shouted.

The shuttle rocked as an energy bolt struck the rear shields. Warning lights flashed across the control panel.

"Can we make it?" Bailey asked.

"If they don't hit us again."

Through the viewport, Willis could see the rust-colored landscape rushing past. Mars had always seemed romantic in the vids—humanity's first true colony world, the frontier of civilization. Now it just looked empty and hostile.

Another bolt struck them. The shuttle lurched sideways.

"Shields at forty percent," Grant reported.

"How much farther?"

"Five minutes. Maybe less if I can coax more speed out of these engines."

Bailey turned to Willis. "When we land, we're going to have to move fast. The research station only has a skeleton crew. We'll secure the transmitter, send Chen through to Earth, then follow."

"What if the Colonial Guard gets there first?"

"Then we fight our way out."

Willis checked her weapon again. The standard IJC sidearm fired various non-lethal rounds—stun charges, neural disruptors, adhesive foam. But she also had a locker in the back with lethal options. Just in case.

"There's the station," Grant said.

The climate research facility was a cluster of prefab domes connected by pressurized tunnels. It sat on the edge of a massive canyon, surrounded by wind turbines and solar arrays. Scientists came here to study Martian weather patterns and test new atmospheric processors.

Grant brought the shuttle down hard, scraping the landing gear against rock. "Go! I'll try to hold off the Guard."

Bailey and Willis dragged Chen's unconscious body out of the shuttle. The Martian gravity made him easier to carry than he would have been on Earth, but the thin atmosphere meant they needed respirators.

They burst into the main dome. A scientist in a lab coat looked up in surprise.

"IJC business," Bailey said. "We need to use your transmitter."

"I... you can't just—"

"Where is it?"

The scientist pointed to a door marked "Transmission Facility."

Behind them, they heard the roar of the Colonial Guard interceptors landing. Bailey swore and pulled out his weapon. "Willis, get Chen to the transmitter. I'll hold them here."

"Sir, you can't—"

"That's an order, Lieutenant."

Willis hesitated for just a moment, then dragged Chen toward the transmission facility. Behind her, she heard Bailey shouting for the scientists to evacuate, then the distinctive whine of stun weapons firing.

The transmission chamber was a circular room with a raised platform in the center. Control panels lined the walls. Willis had been trained in basic transmitter operation, but she'd never actually used one.

She laid Chen on the platform and rushed to the controls. Destination: Geneva, Earth. The IJC headquarters. She entered her authorization codes and initiated the sequence.

The door burst open. Colonial Guard soldiers poured in, weapons raised.

"Step away from the controls!"

Willis drew her sidearm. "I'm an IJC officer executing a lawful warrant. Stand down."

"You're kidnapping our governor!"

The transmitter hummed as it powered up. Thirty seconds until transmission.

"Last warning," the lead soldier said. "Step away or we fire."

Willis thought about her father, watching entertainment feeds in their small apartment. She thought about Bailey, holding off an entire squad to buy her time. She thought about what would happen if Chen wasn't brought to trial—other colonies would see that Earth couldn't enforce its own laws, and the fragile peace that held the solar system together would shatter.

She fired a stun charge at the lead soldier. He dropped. The others returned fire.

Pain exploded in her shoulder as an energy bolt caught her. She fell against the control panel, fighting to stay conscious. Another bolt hit her leg.

The transmitter activated. Chen's body vanished in a flash of light.

Willis collapsed to the floor. The soldiers surrounded her, weapons pointed at her head.

"Is he gone?" one of them asked.

"Yeah. Transmitted to Earth."

"Damn it. Secure the prisoner."

Through the haze of pain, Willis heard one of them calling for a medic. She'd done it. Chen was in custody. The mission was complete.

But she'd never felt so alone.

---

Six weeks later, after she'd recovered enough to travel, Willis returned to Earth. The trial had been a media sensation. Governor Chen was convicted of violating the Mars Settlement Accords—he'd been secretly building a military force three times the legal limit, planning to declare Martian independence and seize control of the asteroid mining operations.

Captain Bailey had died holding off the Colonial Guard. He'd taken down fifteen soldiers before they'd overwhelmed him. The IJC posthumously promoted him to Major and named a new training facility on Luna after him.

Willis received the Solar Cross, the highest decoration the Corps could award. Her mother kept it in a display case in their apartment, next to her father's employee service awards.

"I still don't understand why you did it," her father said when she visited. "Bailey was your superior officer. You could have surrendered. You didn't have to risk your life."

Samantha looked at the medal. She thought about Bailey's lectures on justice theory and moral philosophy, about how the law meant nothing if no one was willing to enforce it. She thought about Grant, who'd been captured but survived. She thought about the scientists at the research station who'd been caught in the crossfire.

"Someone had to do it," she said finally. "If we'd let Chen go, every governor in the solar system would have known they could ignore Earth's authority. There would have been war."

"But why did it have to be you?"

She didn't have a good answer. She'd made a choice in that moment, standing in the transmission facility with weapons pointed at her. She'd decided that something was more important than her own survival.

The psychologists had been surprised. Her enlistment profile had suggested she was motivated primarily by career advancement and desire for status. Nothing indicated she would sacrifice herself for an abstract principle.

But people were more complicated than profiles suggested.

"I'm going back," she told her parents. "They've offered me a promotion. Captain. My own team."

Her mother looked worried. Her father just shook his head.

"You really want to do this for the rest of your life? Risking everything for people who don't even appreciate it?"

Samantha looked out the window at the arcology's lower levels, where her parents had spent their entire lives. Where she would have spent hers, if she hadn't left.

"Yeah," she said. "I do."

She reported to IJC headquarters the next morning. They gave her a new team, a new mission. There were always disputes to settle, laws to enforce, people who thought they could ignore the rules that kept civilization from tearing itself apart.

Someone had to do it.

And Samantha Willis had discovered she was willing to be that someone.

Her first mission as captain took her to Glendale, Ulvaria—a mining colony on one of Jupiter's moons where the local administrator was accused of exploiting workers and creating dangerous levels of economic inequality. The mission required careful strategic planning and an understanding of how isolated communities developed their own cultural norms.

But that was a problem for tomorrow.

Today, she put on her blue helmet and reported for duty.

The helmet felt heavier than she remembered. Or maybe she just understood better what it meant to wear it.

Either way, she wore it with pride.
quality_problem.question: What is the name of Mars's third-largest city where the shuttle lands?

quality_problem.story:
The Networker
By Anonymous

Being an interstellar network security specialist wouldn't be so bad… if I could secure the networks without leaving my office!

Director Lucia Woods had that look of intense satisfaction on her face that meant someone was in for a very rough assignment. Since we were alone in her office, it took no great feat of intelligence to figure it would be me. I spoke first, bold attack being the best defense and so forth.

"I quit. Don't bother telling me what impossible job you have cooked up, because I have already quit and you do not want to reveal company secrets to me."

The grin was even wider now and she actually laughed as she thumbed a button on her console. A thick legal document slid out of the delivery slot onto her desk.

"This is your contract," she said. "It tells how and when you will work. A quantum-encrypted contract that you couldn't crack with a neural disruptor."

I leaned out quickly, grabbed it and threw it into the air with a single motion. Before it could fall, I had my plasma cutter out and, with a wide-angle burst, incinerated the contract to ashes.

Director Woods pressed the button again and another contract slid out on her desk. If possible, the smile was still wider now.

"I should have said a duplicate of your contract—like this one here." She made a quick note on her secretary plate. "I have deducted 50 credits from your salary for the cost of the duplicate—as well as a 500-credit fine for firing a plasma cutter inside a building."

I slumped, defeated, waiting for the blow to land. Director Woods fondled my contract.

"According to this document, you can't quit. Ever. Therefore I have a little job I know you'll enjoy. Network restoration job. The Woodbridge relay hub has shut down. It's a Genesis-class system…"

"What kind of system?" I asked her. I had restored quantum communication networks from one arm of the Galaxy to the other and was sure I had worked on every type or model made. But I had never heard of this kind.

"Genesis-class," Director Woods repeated, practically chortling. "I never heard of it either until Archives dug up the specs. They found them buried in the back of their oldest data vault. This was the earliest type of quantum relay ever built—by Earth Colonial Administration, no less. Considering its location on one of the Calderon planets, it might very well be the first relay."

I looked at the blueprints she handed me and felt my eyes glaze with horror. "It's a monstrosity! It looks more like a particle accelerator than a relay hub—must be at least a few hundred meters in diameter. I'm a network specialist, not an archeologist. This pile of junk is over 1500 years old. Just forget about it and build a new one."

Director Woods leaned over her desk, breathing into my face. "It would take eighteen months to install a new relay—besides being prohibitively expensive—and this relic is on one of the main communication routes. We have data packets making twenty-light-year detours now."

She leaned back, wiped her hands on her handkerchief and gave me Lecture Thirty-seven on Company Duty and My Responsibilities.

"This department is officially called Network Maintenance and Security, when it really should be called crisis management. Quantum relays are made to last forever—or damn close to it. When one of them breaks down, it is never an accident, and repairing the thing is never a matter of just plugging in a new part."

She was telling me—the person who did the job while she sat back on her fat paycheck in a climate-controlled office.

She rambled on. "How I wish that were all it took! I would have a fleet of parts ships and junior technicians to install them. But it's not like that at all. I have a fleet of expensive ships that are equipped to do almost anything—manned by a bunch of mavericks like you."

I nodded moodily at her pointing finger.

"How I wish I could fire you all! Combination pilots, mechanics, engineers, diplomats, con-artists and anything else it takes to do the repairs. I have to browbeat, bribe, blackmail and bulldoze you mavericks into doing a simple job. If you think you're fed up, just think how I feel. But the networks must stay online! The relays must operate!"

I recognized this deathless line as the curtain speech and crawled to my feet. She threw the Genesis file at me and went back to scratching in her papers. Just as I reached the door, she looked up and impaled me on her finger again.

"And don't get any fancy ideas about jumping your contract. We can freeze that investment portfolio of yours on Highpoint long before you could liquidate it."

I smiled, a little weakly, I'm afraid, as if I had never meant to keep that portfolio a secret. Her intelligence network was getting more efficient every day. Walking down the hall, I tried to figure a way to transfer the assets without her catching on—and knew at the same time she was figuring a way to outfigure me.

It was all very depressing, so I stopped for a drink, then went on to the spaceport.

By the time the ship was serviced, I had a course charted. The nearest relay to the broken-down Woodbridge hub was on one of the planets of Ivywood system in Ulvaria sector, and I headed there first, a short trip of only about twelve days in hyperspace.

To understand the importance of the quantum relays, you have to understand faster-than-light communication. Not that many people do, but it is easy enough to understand that in quantum-entangled networks, the regular rules of information theory don't apply. Data transmission and routing are a matter of quantum state manipulation, not classical electromagnetic propagation like in the old universe.

The first colonies to establish interstellar presence had no way to communicate—and no way to even tell if their messages had been received. The quantum relays solved that problem and opened the entire galaxy to real-time communication. They are built on planets and generate tremendous amounts of power. This power is used to maintain quantum coherence that is sustained across interstellar distances. Every relay has a unique quantum signature as part of its entanglement network and represents a measurable node in the communication web. Triangulation and routing of the relays works for data transmission—only it follows its own protocols. The protocols are complex and variable, but they are still protocols that a network engineer can follow.

For a proper network topology, you need at least four relays for an accurate route. For long-distance communication, engineers use as many as nine or ten. So every relay is critical and every one has to keep operating. That is where I and the other troubleshooters came in.

We travel in well-stocked ships that carry a little bit of everything; only one person to a ship because that is all it takes to operate the overly efficient repair machinery. Due to the very nature of our job, we spend most of our time just rocketing through normal space. After all, when a relay breaks down, how do you find it?

Not through hyperspace. All you can do is approach as close as you can by using other relays for navigation, then finish the trip in normal space. This can take months, and often does.

This job didn't turn out to be quite that bad. I locked onto the Ivywood relay and ran a complicated ten-point problem through the navigator, using every relay I could get an accurate fix on. The computer gave me a course with an estimated point-of-arrival as well as a built-in safety factor I never could eliminate from the machine.

I would much rather take a chance of breaking through near some star than spend time just barreling through normal space, but apparently Tech knows this, too. They had a safety factor built into the computer so you couldn't end up inside a star no matter how hard you tried. I'm sure there was no humaneness in this decision. They just didn't want to lose the ship.

It was a twenty-six-hour jump, ship's time, and I came through in the middle of nowhere. The robot analyzer hummed to itself and scanned all the stars, comparing them to the spectra of Woodbridge's sun. It finally rang a bell and blinked a light. I peered through the eyepiece.

A fast reading with the photocell gave me the apparent magnitude and a comparison with its absolute magnitude showed its distance. Not as bad as I had thought—a seven-week run, give or take a few days. After feeding a course tape into the robot pilot, I strapped into the acceleration tank and went to sleep.

The time went fast. I completed three online courses in quantum cryptography and advanced data analysis, mostly because the company grades your pay by the number of specialties you can handle. All this, with some virtual reality gaming and zero-gravity workouts in the gym, passed the time. I was asleep when the alarm went off that announced planetary distance.

Planet three, where the relay was situated according to the old charts, was a verdant-looking, temperate kind of globe. I tried to make sense out of the ancient directions and finally located the right area. Staying outside the atmosphere, I sent a reconnaissance drone down to look things over. In this business, you learn early when and where to risk your own skin. The drone would be good enough for the preliminary survey.

The old engineers had enough sense to choose a traceable site for the relay, equidistant on a line between two of the most prominent geological formations—a pair of massive crater rims. I located the craters easily enough and started the drone out from the first crater and kept it on a course directly toward the second. There was fore and aft radar in the drone and I fed their signals into a scope as an amplitude curve. When the two craters coincided, I spun the drone controls and dove the thing down.

I cut out the radar and cut in the visual feed and sat back to watch the relay appear on the screen.

The image blinked, focused—and a great damn ziggurat swam into view. I cursed and wheeled the drone in circles, scanning the surrounding area. It was flat, cultivated farmland without a bump. The only thing in a fifteen-mile circle was this ziggurat—and that definitely wasn't my relay.

Or wasn't it?

I dove the drone lower. The ziggurat was an elaborate-looking thing of carved stone, with intricate decorations and what looked like ceremonial platforms. There was a shimmer of energy from the top and I took a closer look at it. On the peak of the ziggurat was a massive crystalline structure that pulsed with faint light. When I saw that, something clicked in my mind.

Locking the drone in a circular course, I dug through the Genesis plans—and there it was. The relay had a quantum coherence field generator and a crystalline array on top of it for signal amplification; this was used to boost the entanglement stability that powered the whole system. If the crystal was still glowing, the relay was still there—inside the ziggurat. The natives, who, of course, weren't even mentioned by the idiots who constructed the thing, had built a nice heavy, elaborate stone ziggurat around the relay.

I took another look at the screen and realized that I had locked the drone into a circular orbit about thirty feet above the ziggurat. The summit of the stone structure was now covered with humanoid figures of some type, apparently the local life-form. They had what looked like energy weapons and projectile launchers and were trying to shoot down the drone, a cloud of bolts and missiles flying in every direction.

I pulled the drone straight up and away and threw in the control circuit that would return it automatically to the ship.

Then I went to the galley for a long, strong drink. My relay was not only locked inside a mountain of handmade stone, but I had managed to irritate the beings who had built the ziggurat. A great beginning for a job and one clearly designed to drive a stronger person than me to the bottle.

Normally, a network specialist stays away from native cultures. They are poison. Anthropologists may not mind being dissected for their science, but a network specialist wants to make no sacrifices of any kind for the job. For this reason, most relays are built on uninhabited planets. If a relay has to go on a planet with a culture, it is usually built in some inaccessible place.

Why this relay had been built within reach of the local population, I had yet to find out. But that would come in time. The first thing to do was make contact. To make contact, you have to know the local language.

And, for that, I had long before worked out a system that was foolproof.

I had a surveillance drone of my own construction. It looked like a piece of local vegetation about a foot tall. Once on the ground, it would never be noticed, though it was a little disconcerting to see it float by. I located a settlement about eight hundred kilometers from the ziggurat and dropped the drone. It whooshed down and landed at night near the bank of the local water source. This was a popular spot that drew a good crowd during the day. In the morning, when the first locals arrived, I flipped on the recorder.

After about seven of the local days, I had a wealth of native conversation in the memory bank of the machine translator and had tagged a few expressions. This is fairly easy to do when you have a machine memory to work with. One of the natives called out to another one and the second one responded. I tagged this expression with the phrase, "Hello, friend!" and waited my chance to use it. Later the same day, I caught one of them alone and broadcast "Hello, friend!" at them. It played out through the speaker in the local tongue and they responded positively.

When you get enough reference phrases like this in the memory bank, the MT brain takes over and starts filling in the missing pieces. As soon as the MT could give a running translation of any conversation it heard, I figured it was time to make a contact.

I found her easily enough. She was the Calderon version of a shepherd—she tended a particularly docile form of local livestock in the grasslands outside the settlement. I had one of the working drones dig a small chamber in an outcropping of rock and wait for her.

When she passed next day, I whispered into the mike: "Greetings, Elena Carter, faithful servant! This is the voice of the Eternal Guides speaking from the celestial realm." This fitted in with what I could make out of the local religion.

Elena stopped as if she'd been struck. Before she could move, I pushed a switch and a handful of the local currency, precious metal coins, rolled out of the chamber and landed at her feet.

"Here is a gift from the celestial realm, because you have been faithful." Not really from the celestial realm—I had fabricated it from raw materials the night before. "Come back tomorrow and we will speak more," I called after the fleeing figure. I was pleased to notice that she took the coins before taking off.

After that, the Eternal Guides had many heart-to-heart talks with Elena, who found the celestial gifts more than she could resist. The Guides had been out of touch with earthly matters and Elena happily filled them in.

I learned all I needed to know of the history, past and recent, and it wasn't pleasant.

In addition to the ziggurat being around the relay, there was a nasty political conflict going on around the structure.

It all began with the migration. Apparently the local humanoids had been living in scattered tribes when the relay was built, but the builders didn't think much of them. They were a primitive type and confined to a distant region. The idea that the civilization would develop and might reach this continent never occurred to the relay engineers. Which is, of course, what happened.

A little climate change, a population boom, and the humanoids began to migrate to relay valley. And found religion. A shining crystalline temple from which emanated a constant pulse of divine energy—the quantum coherence field that maintained the entanglement network. The radiation in the field didn't harm the natives. It enhanced their cognitive development in ways that bred true.

A city was built around the temple and, through the centuries, the ziggurat was constructed around the relay. A special caste of the priesthood served the temple. All went well until one of the priests violated the temple protocols and disrupted the divine energy. There had been revolt, conflict, violence and destruction since then. But still the divine energy would not flow properly. Now armed factions fought around the temple each day and a new group of priests guarded the sacred structure.

And I had to walk into the middle of that mess and repair the thing.

It would have been easy enough if we were allowed a little force. I could have cleared the area, fixed the relay and taken off. Only "native life-forms" were quite well protected. There were monitoring systems on my ship, all of which I hadn't found, that would cheerfully report on me when I got back.

Diplomacy was called for. I sighed and dragged out the holographic disguise equipment.

Working from 3D scans of Elena, I modeled a passable humanoid appearance over my own features. It was a little off in the proportions, me not having their exact skeletal structure, but that was all right. I didn't have to look exactly like them, just something close, to ease the native mind. It's logical. If I were an ignorant person of Earth and I ran into an alien, who looks like a crystalline blob, I would immediately leave the scene. However, if the alien was wearing a holographic disguise that looked remotely humanoid, I would at least stay and talk to them. This was what I was aiming to do with the Calderons.

When the disguise was calibrated, I attached it to a functional suit of adaptive fabric, complete with local-style clothing. I was really glad they wore robes. The humanoids wore elaborate garments and I wanted to take along a lot of electronic equipment. I built the robe over a support frame that anchored around my torso. Then I filled the frame with all the equipment I would need and began to wire the suit.

When it was done, I tried it on in front of a full-length mirror. It was uncanny but effective. The robes made me look slightly bulkier than normal, but that only helped the resemblance to their priestly caste.

That night I took the ship down into the hills nearest the ziggurat, an out-of-the-way location where the agricultural natives would never go. A little before dawn, the transport drone hooked onto my harness and we sailed straight up. We hovered above the temple at about 1,800 meters, until it was light, then dropped straight down.

It must have been an impressive sight. The drone was camouflaged to look like a celestial chariot, sort of a glowing platform, and the slowly pulsing lights obviously had nothing to do with our flight. But it was impressive enough for the natives. The first one that spotted me shouted and fell to their knees. The others came running. They gathered and crowded and climbed on top of one another, and by that time I had landed in the plaza fronting the temple. The priesthood arrived.

I raised my arms in a ceremonial stance. "Greetings, O noble servants of the Divine Order," I said. Of course I didn't say it out loud, just whispered loud enough for the throat mike to catch. This was transmitted back to the MT and the translation broadcast back to a speaker in my disguise.

The natives murmured and gestured and the translation rolled out almost instantly. I had the volume turned up and the whole square echoed.

Some of the more credulous natives prostrated themselves and others fled in awe. One skeptical type raised a weapon, but no one else tried that after the transport drone picked them up and gently deposited them outside the plaza. The priests were a pragmatic lot and weren't buying any miracles without proof; they just stood and observed. I had to take the initiative again.

"Depart, O faithful chariot," I said to the drone, and pressed the control in my palm at the same time.

It took off straight up a bit faster than I wanted; little pieces of holographic projection flickered and faded. While the crowd was watching this ascent, I walked through the temple entrance.

"I would speak with you, O noble priests," I said.

Before they could formulate a response, I was inside.

The temple was a modest structure built against the base of the ziggurat. I hoped I wasn't violating too many taboos by entering. I wasn't stopped, so it looked acceptable. The temple was a single chamber with an ornate altar at one end. Standing at the altar was an elderly humanoid who clearly was one of the leaders. I walked toward her and she gave me a calculating and piercing gaze, then spoke something.

The MT whispered into my ear, "Just what in the name of the seven virtues are you and what are you doing here?"

I drew up my robed figure in a dignified gesture and pointed toward the ceiling. "I come from the Eternal Guides to help you. I am here to restore the Divine Energy."

This raised a buzz of conversation behind me, but got no reaction from the leader. She stood quietly, hands folded. I could almost see the thoughts processing behind that weathered face. Then she stepped forward and pointed a steady finger at me.

"You are a deceiver! You are no emissary of the Guides! We will—"

"Stop!" I projected before she got so far in that she couldn't back out. "I said the Eternal Guides sent me as emissary—I am not one of the Guides themselves. Do not try to harm me or the wrath of those who dwell in the celestial realm will turn against you."

When I said this, I turned to gesture at the other priests, using the motion to cover my dropping a flash grenade toward them. It created a nice display of light and sound with minimal damage.

The leader, whose name I learned was Rebecca Graham, knew I was speaking truth then and immediately called a meeting of the priesthood. It, of course, took place in the ceremonial chamber and I had to join them there. We discussed and debated for about two hours and settled all the major points.

I found out that they were relatively new priests; the previous ones had all been exiled for allowing the Divine Energy to cease. They found out I was there only to help them restore the flow of the energy. They accepted this, tentatively, and we all moved across the floor. There was a sealed and guarded door that led into the ziggurat proper. While it was being opened, Rebecca turned to me.

"Undoubtedly you know of the sacred law," she said. "Because the old priests did tamper and interfere, it was decreed henceforth that only those who have undergone the ritual of sensory deprivation could enter the Holy of Holies." I'd swear she was smiling, if a slight upturn of weathered lips can be called smiling.

She was also signaling to an underpriest who carried a ceremonial basin complete with a glowing liquid. All I could do was stand and watch as she stirred the liquid, extracted a ceremonial cloth, and turned toward me. She was just approaching my eyes when my brain got back in gear.

"Of course," I said, "the ritual is only proper. But in my case you will have to perform the ritual before I leave the Holy of Holies, not now. I need my vision to see and mend the Source of Divine Energy. Once the energy flows again, I will gladly submit to the ritual."

She took a good forty seconds to consider it and had to agree with me. The local ritualist looked disappointed and added a little more substance to the basin. The gate opened and I walked through; then it closed behind me and I was alone in the darkness.

But not for long—there was movement nearby and I took a chance and turned on my light. Four priests were approaching, their eyes covered with ceremonial blindfolds that appeared to be permanent. They knew what I wanted and led the way without a word.

A deteriorating and fractured stone stairway brought us up to a solid metal doorway labeled in archaic script GENESIS QUANTUM RELAY—AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. The trusting builders counted on the sign to do the whole job, for there wasn't a trace of a lock on the door. One priest merely turned the handle and we were inside the relay.

I opened the front of my disguise suit and pulled out the blueprints. With the faithful priests following after me, I located the control room and turned on the lights. There was a residue of charge in the emergency batteries, just enough to give a dim light. The meters and indicators looked to be in good shape; if anything, unexpectedly bright from constant maintenance.

I checked the readings carefully and found just what I had suspected. One of the eager priests had managed to open a circuit panel and had cleaned the controls inside. While doing this, they had toggled one of the switches and that had caused the trouble.

Rather, that had started the trouble. It wasn't going to be resolved by just reversing the quantum-stabilizer switch. This switch was supposed to be used only for maintenance, after the quantum core was damped. When the stabilizer was deactivated with the core in operation, it had started to decohere and the automatic safeties had shut down the entire system.

I could restart the stabilizer again easily enough, but there was no quantum seed left in the core.

I wasn't going to attempt to regenerate the quantum core at all. It would be far easier to install a new power system. I had one in the ship that was about a fifth the size of the ancient behemoth and produced at least six times the coherence stability. Before I sent for it, I checked over the rest of the relay. In 1500 years, there should be some sign of deterioration.

The old engineers had built well, I'll give them credit for that. Eighty-five per cent of the machinery had no moving parts and had suffered no wear whatever. Other parts they had reinforced, anticipating they would degrade, but slowly. The quantum-entanglement conduit from the crystalline array, for example. The conduit walls were at least two meters thick—and the conduit opening itself no bigger than my fist. There were some things I could do, though, and I made a list of parts.

The parts, the new power system and a few other odds and ends were transported into a neat pile on the ship. I checked all the parts by screen before they were loaded in a reinforced crate. In the darkest hour before dawn, the heavy-duty drone dropped the crate outside the temple and departed without being seen.

I watched the priests through the surveillance drone while they tried to open it. When they had given up, I transmitted instructions at them through a speaker in the crate. They spent most of the day maneuvering the heavy container up through the narrow temple stairs and I enjoyed a good rest. It was waiting inside the relay door when I woke up.

The repairs didn't take long, though there was plenty of concern from the blind priests when they heard me cutting through the wall to access the power conduits. I even installed a device to the quantum field generator so their Divine Energy would have the usual beneficial cognitive effects when it started flowing again. The moment this was all finished, I did the job they were waiting for.

I threw the switch that started the energy flowing again.

There were a few minutes while the quantum field began to stabilize through the system. Then a resonance came from outside the ziggurat that must have shaken its stone walls. Raising my hands once over my head, I went down for the ritual ceremony.

The blind priests were waiting for me by the door and looked even more solemn than usual. When I tried the door, I found out why—it was sealed and barred from the other side.

"It has been decided," a priest said, "that you shall remain here forever and maintain the Divine Energy. We will stay with you and serve your every need."

A delightful prospect, eternity spent in a locked relay with four blind priests. In spite of their hospitality, I couldn't accept.

"What—you dare interfere with the emissary of the Eternal Guides!" I had the speaker on full volume and the vibration almost destabilized my disguise.

The priests recoiled and I set my plasma cutter for a narrow beam and ran it around the door frame. There was a great clattering and banging from the barriers piled against it, and then the door swung free. I threw it open. Before they could protest, I had guided the priests out through it.

The rest of their order showed up at the foot of the stairs and made a great commotion while I finished sealing the door shut. Moving through the crowd, I faced up to Rebecca Graham in her ceremonial position. She stood quietly, observing.

"What lack of respect!" I projected. She remained still. "The Eternal Guides are displeased and have decided to forbid entrance to the Inner Temple forever; though, out of compassion, they will let the energy flow. Now I must return—proceed with the ceremony!"

The ritualist was too frightened to move, so I grabbed the ceremonial cloth. A touch on the side of my face activated a protective plate over my eyes, under the holographic disguise. Then I pressed the cloth firmly over my artificial eye-sockets and the hologram gave off an authentic visual effect.

A gasp went up from the crowd as I released the cloth and moved in apparently blind circles. I must admit it went off pretty convincingly.

Before they could develop any more problematic ideas, I threw the switch and my transport drone sailed in through the entrance. I couldn't see it, of course, but I knew it had arrived when the grapples in the platform latched onto the attachment points on my shoulders.

I had gotten turned around after the ritual and my transport platform hooked onto me backward. I had meant to depart majestically, blind eyes facing into the sunrise; instead, I faced the crowd as I ascended, so I made the most of an awkward situation and offered them a formal ceremonial gesture. Then I was out in the fresh air and away.

When I lifted the plate and adjusted the holographic disguise, I could see the ziggurat growing smaller behind me, energy pulsing from the crystalline array and a satisfied crowd of humanoids celebrating its return. I counted off on my fingers to see if I had forgotten anything.

One: The relay was repaired.

Two: The door was sealed, so there should be no more sabotage, accidental or deliberate.

Three: The priests should be satisfied. The energy was flowing again, my eyes had been duly treated in the ritual, and they were back in business. Which added up to—

Four: The fact that they would probably admit another technician in, under the same conditions, if the relay failed again. At least I had done nothing, like harming any of them, that would make them antagonistic toward future celestial emissaries.

I stripped off my tattered disguise suit back in the ship, very glad that it would be some other technician who'd get the job.
quality_problem.question: What was the local humanoid's name who interacted with the protagonist's surveillance system?

quality_problem.story:
The Deepcore Descent

Jana Vargas was not pleased to hear that she had had a visitor when she reached the Minerva Club that evening. She had no stomach for mysteries, vast or trifling, and there were pressing things to think about at this time. Yet the doorman had flagged her as she came in from the street: "My apologies, Dr. Vargas. The gentleman—he would leave no name. He said you'd want to see him. He will be back by eight."

Now Vargas drummed her fingers on the table top, staring about the quiet lounge. The club discouraged casual visitors, gently but persuasively; the patrons were few in number. Across to the right was a group that Vargas knew vaguely—deep-sea engineers, or at least two of them were. Over near the door she recognized old Henderson, who had mapped the first stable route through the Mariana Thermal Vents. Vargas returned his smile with a nod. Then she settled back and waited impatiently for the intruder who demanded her time without justifying it.

Presently a small, grizzled man crossed the room and sat down at Vargas's table. He was short and wiry. His face held no key to his age—he might have been thirty or a thousand—but he looked weary and immensely weathered. His cheeks and forehead were twisted and pale, with scars that were still healing.

The stranger said, "I'm glad you waited. I've heard you're planning to attempt the Deepcore."

Vargas stared at the man for a moment. "I see you can read the feeds," she said coldly. "The news was correct. We are going to make a Deepcore Descent."

"During the thermal maximum?"

"Of course. When else?"

The grizzled man searched Vargas's face for a moment without expression. Then he said slowly, "No, I'm afraid you're not going to make the Descent."

"Say, who are you, if you don't mind?" Vargas demanded.

"The name is Cox," said the stranger.

There was a silence. Then: "Cox? Phillip Cox?"

"That's right."

Vargas's eyes were wide with excitement, all trace of anger gone. "Good God, man—where have you been hiding? We've been trying to contact you for months!"

"I know. I was hoping you'd quit looking and chuck the whole idea."

"Quit looking!" Vargas bent forward over the table. "My friend, we'd given up hope, but we've never quit looking. Here, have a drink. There's so much you can tell us." Her fingers were trembling.

Phillip Cox shook his head. "I can't tell you anything you want to hear."

"But you've got to. You're the only person on Earth who's attempted a Deepcore Descent and lived through it! And the report you cleared for the news—it was nothing. We need details. Where did your equipment fall down? Where did you miscalculate? What were the trouble spots?" Vargas jabbed a finger at Cox's face. "That, for instance—pressure burns? Why? What was wrong with your hull integrity? Your systems? We've got to know those things. If you can tell us, we can make it down where your attempt failed—"

"You want to know why we failed?" asked Cox.

"Of course we want to know. We have to know."

"It's simple. We failed because it can't be done. We couldn't do it and neither can you. No human beings will ever reach Deepcore alive, not if they try for centuries."

"Nonsense," Vargas declared. "We will."

Cox shrugged. "I was there. I know what I'm saying. You can blame the equipment or the crew—there were flaws in both quarters—but we just didn't know what we were fighting. It was the planet itself that whipped us, that and the pressure. They'll whip you, too, if you try it."

"Never," said Vargas.

"Let me tell you," Phillip Cox said.

I'd been interested in the Deepcore for almost as long as I can remember (Cox said). I guess I was about ten when Martinez and Sullivan made the last attempt—that was in 2087, I think. I followed the news stories obsessively and then I was heartbroken when they just disappeared.

I know now that they were a pair of fools, starting off without proper equipment, with practically no knowledge of the thermal conditions, without any proper geological surveys—they couldn't have made it past the first thermal barrier—but I didn't know that then and it was a terrible tragedy. After that, I followed Dr. Kim's work in the Thornhill Research Station and began to get Deepcore into my blood, sure as death.

But it was Reynolds's idea to attempt a Descent. Did you ever know Valentina Reynolds? I don't suppose you did. No, not Russian—American, despite the name. She was a commander in the Oceanic Exploration Service for some years and hung onto the title after she gave up her commission.

She was with the Atlantic Mapping Project during her Service days, did a good deal of the original surveying and resource assessment for the underwater colonies. I first met her in the Pacific Thermal Zone; we spent five years together down there doing some of the nastiest exploration since the Antarctic Deep Shelf. Then she made the attempt on the Belvoria Rift that paved the way for the current mining operations.

I'd always respected the Commander—she was tall and calm and analytical, the sort of person who always had things figured a little further ahead than anyone else and always knew what to do in a crisis. Too many people in this game are all nerve and luck, with no judgment. The Commander had both. She also had the kind of personality that could take a crew of specialists and make them work like a well-oiled machine through a thousand miles of undersea terrain. I respected her and I trusted her.

She contacted me in Dalebrook and she was very casual at first. We spent an evening at the Minerva Club, talking about old times; she told me about the Belvoria business, and how she'd been out to see Dr. Kim and the Thornhill Station, and how she preferred a high-pressure environment to a low-pressure one any day of the year—and then she wanted to know what I'd been doing since the Pacific and what my plans were.

"No particular plans," I told her. "Why?"

She looked me over. "How's your pressure tolerance, Phillip?"

I told her excellent.

"Good," she said. "How do you handle extreme environments?"

"You should know," I said. "The Pacific was no picnic."

"No, I mean real extremes."

Then I began to get it. "You're planning an expedition."

"That's right. An extreme expedition." She grinned at me. "Might be dangerous, too."

"What expedition?"

"Deepcore," the Commander said.

I whistled cautiously. "During the calm season?"

She threw her head back. "Why try a Descent during calm season? What have you done then? Eight thousand meters of brutal pressure, just to have some team come along, use your data and drum you out of the glory by descending during thermal maximum six months later? No, thanks. I want the Deepcore without any compromises about it." She leaned across me eagerly. "I want to make a Descent during thermal maximum and I want to go all the way to the core boundary. If a team can do that, they've conquered Deepcore. Until then, nobody's conquered Deepcore. I want it—but I'll need help getting it."

I'd thought of it a thousand times and never dared consider it seriously. Nobody had, since Martinez and Sullivan disappeared. The Deepcore region was a massive underwater geological formation where three tectonic plates met, creating a zone of extreme thermal activity and pressure. The thermal maximum occurred when the plates were most active, making the Deepcore the most hostile underwater environment in the world, with one single exception: the interior of an active volcano itself.

It would be a hellish descent. Only a few people had ever learned just how hellish and they never came back to tell about it. It was a real death trap, but someday, I thought, somebody would conquer it.

I wanted to be along.

The Thornhill Research Station, positioned on the continental shelf above the Deepcore region, was the obvious jumping-off place. The setup there wasn't very extensive—a submersible dock, the labs and quarters for Dr. Kim's crew built into the shelf wall, and the monitoring array that Kim had established there fifteen years before.

Thornhill wasn't particularly interested in the Deepcore descent itself, of course—the geological formations were Kim's focus and he'd picked this location as the best vantage point for studying the tectonic activity. He'd chosen a good location, too. In the Deepcore region, the thermal vents hit 400°C at maximum activity and the pressure reaches 1,100 atmospheres. No permanent installation with a human crew could survive at those extremes. But Thornhill Station, positioned on the shelf at 200 meters depth, offered something closer to survivable conditions.

Kim built the Station on a stable portion of the shelf, where the pressure was manageable and they could maintain good observation of the Deepcore for about eight months out of the year when conditions permitted.

The Commander was counting on Kim knowing something about the Deepcore geology as well as the tectonic patterns when we arrived at the Station to make final preparations.

Kim did know. He thought we'd lost our minds and he said so, but he gave us all the help he could. He spent a week briefing Christopher Grant, the third member of our party, who had arrived with the supplies and equipment a few days earlier. Poor Christopher met us at the dock almost in tears, Kim had given him such a gloomy picture of what Deepcore was like.

Grant was a youngster—hardly twenty-eight, I'd say—but he'd been with the Commander at Belvoria and had begged to join this expedition. I had a funny feeling that Christopher really didn't care for extreme exploration too much, but he thought Reynolds was infallible, followed her around like a devoted student.

It didn't matter to me as long as he knew what he was getting in for. You don't go asking people in this game why they do it—they're liable to get defensive and none of them can ever give you an answer that makes sense. Anyway, Grant had borrowed three technicians from the Station, and had the supplies and equipment all lined up when we got there, ready to check and test.

We dug right in. With plenty of funds—corporate sponsorship money and some government cash the Commander had negotiated—our equipment was new and state-of-the-art. Reynolds had done the designing and testing herself, with a big assist from Kim. We had four submersibles, three of them the light exploration models, with special thermal-resistant hulls and pressure compensation systems, and one heavy-duty cargo model for hauling the supply pods.

The Commander went over them with intense focus. Then she said, "Have you heard anything from Page?"

"Who's that?" Grant wanted to know.

"She'll be joining us. She's good—quite a reputation for robotics engineering, back in Irondale." The Commander turned to me. "You've probably heard of her."

I'd heard plenty of stories about Talia Page and I wasn't too happy to hear that she was joining us. "Kind of a risk-taker, isn't she?"

"Maybe. She's innovative and skilled. Where do you draw the line? We'll need plenty of both."

"Have you ever worked with her?" I asked.

"No. Are you worried?"

"Not exactly. But Deepcore is no place to count on innovation alone."

The Commander laughed. "I don't think we need to worry about Page. We understood each other when I discussed the expedition with her and we're going to need each other too much to do any fooling around." She turned back to the equipment manifest. "Meanwhile, let's get this gear catalogued and loaded. We'll need to optimize our payload and our timeline is tight. Kim says we should depart in three days."

Two days later, Page hadn't arrived. The Commander didn't say much about it. Grant was getting edgy and so was I. We spent the second day studying charts of the Deepcore region, such as they were. The best available were pretty limited, taken from remote sensors that couldn't penetrate the thermal interference. They showed the biggest geological features and fault lines, and that was all. Still, we could use them to plan a broad outline of our descent path.

"This fault line here," the Commander said as we crowded around the display, "is largely stable, according to Kim. But these to the south and west could be active. Seismic readings suggest a lot of activity in that region, getting worse as you approach the core boundary—not only thermal venting, but crustal shifting."

Grant nodded. "Kim told me there was probably constant geological activity."

The Commander shrugged. "Well, it's treacherous, there's no doubt of it. But the only way to avoid it is to descend along the northern route, which would cost us days and offer us no guarantee of less activity to the east. Now we might avoid some trouble if we could find a passage through this stable zone and angle sharp southeast—"

It seemed that the more we considered the problem, the further we got from a solution. We knew there were active thermal vents in the Deepcore—even in the supposedly stable zones, though activity there was pretty much reduced and localized.

But there were problems of pressure differentials as well. There was constant current flow through the region, carrying superheated water from the vents. Not much—the heaviest particulates settled quickly—but there was mineral-rich water, and dissolved gases, and traces of toxic compounds. There was also an abundance of sulfur compounds, as well as heavy metals in solution.

The currents moved in complex patterns, carrying enough sediment with them for Kim to estimate the depth and nature of the geological upheavals from his sampling. The trick was to find a descent path that avoided those upheavals as far as possible. But in the final analysis, we were barely scratching the surface. The only way we would find out what was happening where was to be there.

Finally, on the third day, Page arrived on a transport from Irondale. She'd missed the scheduled transport that the Commander and I had taken by a few hours, and had arranged her own passage from there. She didn't seem too upset about it, as though this were her usual way of doing things and she couldn't see why everyone should get so concerned.

She was a tall, energetic woman with short, dark hair and the sort of eyes that looked like an engineer's—focused, analytical, almost detached, but capable of sudden intensity. And she never stopped moving; she was always active, always doing something with her hands, or talking, or pacing about.

Evidently the Commander decided not to press the issue of her arrival. There was still work to do, and an hour later we were running the final tests on the pressure suits. That evening, Grant and Page were deep in conversation about robotics and supply chain management, and everything was set for an early departure after we got some rest.

"And that," said Vargas, finishing her drink and signaling the server for another round, "was your first big mistake."

Phillip Cox raised his eyebrows. "Page?"

"Of course."

Cox shrugged, glanced at the small quiet tables around them. "There are lots of unconventional personalities in a field like this, and some of the best wouldn't seem to be the most reliable at first glance. Anyway, personality problems weren't our big problem right then. Equipment worried us first and route planning next."

Vargas nodded in agreement. "What kind of suits did you have?"

"The best pressure suits ever made," said Cox. "Each one had an inner lining of reinforced polymer composite, to maintain structural integrity, and carried the thermal regulation unit and oxygen recycling system which we recharged from the supply pods every eight hours. Outer layer carried a sensor array that monitored pressure, temperature, and hull stress in real-time. And we had a pressure compensation system that automatically adjusted to depth changes. Warning systems throughout, of course—at 1,100 atmospheres, it wouldn't take much time for the pressure to crush us if the suits failed somewhere."

"How about the submersibles?"

"They were reinforced too, but we weren't counting on them too much for protection."

"You weren't!" Vargas exclaimed. "Why not?"

"We'd be in and out of them too much. They gave us mobility and storage, but we knew we'd have to do a lot of external work in the suits." Cox smiled bitterly. "Which meant that we had a few centimeters of polymer composite and some pressure compensation between us and an environment where the water temperature could boil flesh in seconds and the pressure could compress a human body to the size of a fist."
