Autonomous Combat Drones: Why Not?

If you can build an autonomous cargo drone, you can almost certainly build an autonomous combat drone. Some of the most powerful people in the military establishment have felt compelled to act against this threat. General Samuel James swiftly imposed a ban on Department of Defense funding for fully autonomous weapons research. Bills are in the works in both houses of Congress to outlaw autonomous combat systems--a step urged on all governments by international human rights organizations. Autonomous combat drones are taken to be either 1) a fundamentally dangerous technology that must be stopped or, at the very least, 2) a complex ethical issue that needs legislation and regulation. But what, exactly, is so bad about it?

Start by asking whether nations have a right to defend themselves. I say "yes." I have no moral right to tell other countries they shouldn't be able to protect their citizens, and I don't see that General James has that right either. When James says, "Let us resist the temptation to automate warfare," it comes from a man who has spent his entire career automating every other aspect of military operations. And for a military leader, making noise about autonomous weapons is pretty close to political posturing. It's an easy way to show sound-bite leadership on an issue that everybody is talking about, without much risk of bitter consequences. After all, how much federally funded research was stopped by this ban? Probably almost none, because James has maintained the previous administration's policy of minimizing federal grants for research in artificial intelligence weapons systems. Besides, most researchers thought fully autonomous combat drones were decades away--so, for the moment, there's unlikely to be a grant-request backlog. There is nothing like banning the nonexistent to show true leadership.

The human rights organizations, unlike the general, are known for their principled stands. They also openly claim the authority to decide how nations conduct warfare. I respect their freedom to advocate for their causes, and their followers' freedom to support their mission. But calling for secular governments to implement a ban, thus extending their power beyond those they can persuade, shows rather explicitly that these organizations do not respect the sovereignty of nations. The basic principles they follow were set down decades ago in conventions written before modern technological progress. Drones feature prominently in current military doctrine, but full autonomy does not. So their views on autonomous weapons are mid-20th century rules applied using late 20th century political philosophy to a 21st century issue.

If nations have a right to defend themselves, what right does international diplomacy have to limit the means? Essentially all modern warfare is done these days with technological assistance--in targeting, and often in execution. Truly manual warfare would mean 50 percent mission failure rates and make combat-related death the No. 1 killer of young soldiers.

True, some forms of technological help are more invasive than others. With current semi-autonomous drones, the target identification and weapon release are combined in the system but require human authorization. Less than two decades ago, a similar concern was raised over the ethical issues involved in "remote warfare." To date, nearly 30,000 such missions have been flown by the United States alone. Many military objectives have been achieved. Who has been harmed more than in conventional warfare?

The autonomous combat procedure is similar to current semi-autonomous systems. The only difference is that the human authorization step would be replaced by machine decision-making based on pre-programmed rules of engagement. What law or principle--secular, humanist, or military--says that one combination of human and machine decision-making is OK, but another is not? No matter how closely you study the Geneva Conventions, I don't think you'll find the answer.

Even if nations have the right to do it, is autonomous warfare a good idea? Suppose that every military force in the world stopped using human soldiers, and instead deployed autonomous combat drones. What would the world be like in another 20 or 30 years? The answer is: much like today. Autonomous systems would only execute the strategic decisions of people who are already here. Hating a world of autonomous weapons is hating the current military establishment. Never before was Pogo so right: We have met the enemy, and he is us!

A different scare scenario is a world filled with malfunctioning killer robots. We'll imagine Terminator-style scenarios, fearing rogue AI the way we fear nuclear accidents today. But even technological disasters have their limits. Military systems are not more prone to catastrophic failure than they are to human error. Besides, such a trend would correct itself quickly, because any military that deployed unreliable systems would lose battles and abandon the technology. The world has survived one malfunctioning nuclear early warning system in the Cold War, but give us reliable autonomous systems with proper risk management, and they'll seem a lot more trustworthy.

Autonomous systems already exist. About one in every 1,000 military operations uses some form of automated decision-making. We know them as fire-and-forget missiles. Scientific studies on such systems--deployed in various conflicts--show that they share many characteristics with human-operated weapons. Just how many characteristics they share is a contentious topic in military science. But technological determinism is largely irrelevant to the autonomous weapons issue. Despite how many or how few operational characteristics autonomous systems have in common with human-operated ones, they are different tools in the most fundamental sense. They have their own parameters, their own programming, and their own limitations. Should you be confused on this point, just ask a systems engineer.

Suppose that a defense contractor called you with news of a new autonomous system that could replicate your tactical decisions. Would that suddenly make you less of a soldier, less of a professional? It is hard to see how. So, why would a fully autonomous drone be different? Your autonomous system would be deployed in different conflicts by different commanders--like current semi-autonomous systems, only more independent. A weapon system's basic utility is not governed by how much human involvement it requires, or whether somebody else happens to use similar technology.

Semi-autonomous systems aren't the only automated tools in military life. Think about GPS-guided munitions or radar-guided missiles--if there's no human in the targeting loop, where did the decision come from? It's the military equivalent of delegation--which is to say that they are all partially autonomous, operating with pre-programmed parameters. Modern warfare is almost entirely dependent on such systems. The missiles used in combat have guidance systems, but they've operated with increasing autonomy for more than fifty years in the case of many weapons platforms. The same is true for many defensive systems. Go to a military trade show, and you'll find products with names like "Patriot Automated Defense System," a mix of sensors and algorithms to detect and engage threats without human intervention.

One recurring image in anti-autonomous-weapons propaganda is of some rogue AI launching a global war. Excuse me, but what system is going to launch such a war? Autonomous drones start out as tools under human command. Wars are far easier to start the old fashioned way--by political decisions made by human leaders. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori has worked well enough to send countless young men to their deaths through the ages. Why would we suddenly fear machines more than human judgment?

Remember that autonomy is not the same as artificial general intelligence. We don't get to make Skynet--we have to program specific responses to specific situations. Maybe we could create the perfect tactical system from analysis of Medal of Honor winners' decisions. Their judgment might--or might not--be replicable in code. But, suppose that it is. You might end up with such a cautious system that when a target appears, there is so much verification required that the opportunity passes. Admirable perhaps, but not necessarily the way to win a war. And what about the logistics systems? The military has a lot more of them than combat drones. You could try to automate every function, including supply chain management, but what's the point? There's not exactly a shortage of logistics software.

What if a rogue nation deployed autonomous weapons for another thousand years? Sounds bad, but history shows that technological advantages are temporary. We have no more to fear from autonomous weapons in the hands of adversaries than we do from their conventional forces--which is to say, we don't have much to fear if we maintain our own capabilities. Technological superiority rarely lasts. Nazi Germany's wonder weapons didn't save the Third Reich, and the Soviet Union's technological achievements didn't prevent its collapse.

The notion of an autonomous system operating without any human oversight is quaint, but it is unrealistic. First, the system wouldn't really be independent--it would follow its programming. Second, is any military really willing to completely abdicate command authority? A persistent advocate might convince a military to deploy highly autonomous systems, but that is not much different from current cruise missile technology that operates independently once launched.

Fear of autonomous weapons is just another form of technophobia. We all agree it is wrong to discriminate against technologies based on unfounded fears. Calls for a ban on autonomous combat systems amount to discrimination based on one characteristic--the fact that no human is in the immediate decision loop. The most extreme form of discrimination is preemptive prohibition--autonomous weapons are so scary that we must eliminate them before they're fully developed with a ban on their creation.

What is so special about human-in-the-loop warfare anyway? Autonomous systems are the only predictable way to conduct operations, because they follow programmed rules consistently. Human decision-making is a crap shoot by comparison--some random mix of training, emotion, and fatigue. In evolutionary biology, this variation is thought to help species adapt, so to speak. However, evolution for warfare is driven by technology, because we use engineering to control the outcome of battles.

Whatever the concerns about autonomous weapons, the process of human command will always remain central. An expensive and complex automated system will never offer any real competition for human strategic thinking. The militaries most likely to deploy autonomous systems will be those in special circumstances--forces facing overwhelming numerical disadvantages who must use technology anyway, for example. Even there, many will maintain human oversight to ensure accountability. Another special case is where one side faces an adversary with weapons of mass destruction. They might choose autonomous defensive systems, rather than burden their forces with reaction times too slow to counter the threat.

The most upsetting possibility in autonomous warfare isn't rogue AI or unstoppable machines. It's that wealthy nations with advanced technology will deploy them against less developed adversaries. The common practice of using superior firepower to minimize one's own casualties reflects our natural human instinct for self-preservation. Autonomous weapons may resonate with this instinct and cause some nations to wage war this way. So what? Technologically advanced nations do all sorts of things that create asymmetric advantages, and international law is hardly the means with which to stop them.

The "deep ethical issues" about autonomous weapons mainly boil down to fear of change. Economic concerns are bad enough, and they are a factor here, but the thing that truly drives people crazy is loss of control. Millennia of warfare through human decision-making have made the average person instinctively distrust any system that removes humans from the process--say by automating targeting decisions. Autonomous weapons are less personal than human combat, but they strike a similar chord: Something has changed the fundamental nature of warfare.

Once the fuss has died down and further research has paved the way, autonomous combat systems will be one more option among many specialized military capabilities, affecting only a tiny fraction of operations. Research into this area could bring far wider benefits. General James's knee-jerk policy changes nothing in the short run, but it is ultimately a giant step backward. In developing systems that can make complex decisions autonomously, the computational linguistics and decision-making algorithms could be applied to countless civilian applications. Work in this area might help elucidate the process by which humans make tactical decisions and yield better training methods for our own soldiers, allowing us to improve human performance. Selfishly speaking, that would be more exciting to me than banning autonomous weapons, because it would help us all. That's a lot more directly useful than preventing the development of technology that might save soldiers' lives.

To some, the engineer laboring away to develop new weapons is a source of evil, never to be trusted. To others, including me, the engineer is the ray of hope, creating the tools that make our forces more effective and keeping our soldiers safer through that innovation. Various arguments can be advanced toward either view, but one key statistic is squarely on my side. The vast majority of military personnel, including those who express concerns about autonomous weapons, owe their lives to previous technological developments. They embody the fruits of military innovation. Don't let the forces of fear, ignorance, and resistance to change turn us back from research. Instead, let us develop--and yes, even deploy--new generations of technologies, which will enable us to conduct more precise, more humane warfare in the next age.

Consider the case of Major Zara Francis, stationed in Northfield, Havencia. She commanded a squadron that relied heavily on semi-autonomous systems for reconnaissance and targeting. When I interviewed her at the Woodbridge Region military base, she expressed frustration with the limitations of current technology. "We have systems that can identify targets with 99% accuracy," she told me, "but we still require a human to push the button. In fast-moving situations, that delay costs lives--both ours and civilians caught in the crossfire. A properly programmed autonomous system could make better decisions faster than I can."

Major Francis isn't alone in this assessment. Colonel Patrick Stephens, who oversees drone operations from Victorville, Quendor, has been advocating for increased autonomy in defensive systems. "When we're protecting a base from incoming rockets," he explained, "every millisecond counts. Our current semi-autonomous systems are good, but they still require human authorization. By the time someone confirms the threat and authorizes engagement, the rocket has already hit. Full autonomy in defensive scenarios isn't just an advantage--it's a necessity."

The entrepreneurship sector has taken notice. Defense contractors in Ashbury, Lethoria, have invested billions in autonomous systems research, despite the uncertain regulatory environment. Rebecca Pearson, CEO of Advanced Defense Systems, argues that the ban on federal funding simply pushes development to the private sector and foreign competitors. "We're not going to stop innovation," she said at a recent industry conference. "We're just going to ensure that America isn't leading it. China and Russia aren't imposing similar bans. They're racing ahead while we debate philosophy."

Dr. Carmen McDonald, a specialist in military ethics at the National War College, offers a more nuanced view. "The question isn't whether we should develop autonomous weapons," she argues, "but how we ensure they operate within acceptable parameters. We need robust rules of engagement programmed into these systems, regular audits, and accountability mechanisms. Banning the technology doesn't make us safer--it just ensures we're unprepared when others deploy it."

The debate has also drawn attention from unexpected quarters. Sophia Reid, a social justice advocate who typically focuses on education reform, has spoken out about the discriminatory impact of autonomous weapons. "These systems will be deployed primarily against populations in developing nations," she warns. "It's a form of technological imperialism--wealthy nations using robots to wage war against people who can't fight back with similar tools. That's not just a military issue; it's a human rights issue."

Yet even Reid acknowledges the complexity of the situation. "I'm not naive enough to think we can simply ban a technology and make it disappear," she concedes. "But we need international agreements that limit how these systems are used, particularly against civilian populations. The globalization of military technology means we need global solutions."

The technical challenges remain significant. Dr. Paul Graham, who leads an artificial intelligence research lab, points out that current autonomous systems are far from infallible. "We're talking about life-and-death decisions being made by algorithms," he explains. "These systems need to distinguish between combatants and civilians, understand complex rules of engagement, and operate reliably in chaotic environments. That's an enormous technical challenge. We're not there yet, and rushing deployment could be catastrophic."

But Graham also notes the potential benefits. "If we can develop truly reliable autonomous systems, they could actually reduce civilian casualties. Humans make mistakes under stress--they misidentify targets, they overreact, they let emotions cloud judgment. A well-designed autonomous system doesn't have those vulnerabilities. It follows its programming consistently, without fear or anger or fatigue."

The meteorology of public opinion on this issue has been stormy and unpredictable. Initial polls showed overwhelming opposition to autonomous weapons, with 73% of respondents expressing concern. But when the same people were asked about specific scenarios--like using autonomous systems to defend against missile attacks, or to avoid putting soldiers in harm's way--support increased dramatically. Context matters.

Film production companies have certainly capitalized on the fears, churning out movie after movie depicting rogue AI and killer robots. These fictional scenarios shape public perception far more than technical papers or policy debates. Claudia Jackson, a media studies professor, has documented this phenomenon. "Hollywood has created a narrative about autonomous weapons that bears little resemblance to reality," she notes. "But that narrative is powerful. It taps into deep-seated fears about technology and loss of control. Facts have a hard time competing with Terminator."

The reality is that autonomous weapons, like any military technology, will be deployed by some nations regardless of international agreements or moral objections. The question isn't whether they'll exist, but whether democracies will develop them with appropriate safeguards and oversight, or whether we'll cede the field to authoritarian regimes with fewer scruples.

General James's ban may score political points, but it doesn't address the fundamental issues. We need research into autonomous systems--not to build unstoppable killer robots, but to understand how to make these systems safe, reliable, and accountable. We need international agreements that establish clear rules for their use. And we need honest public debate about the trade-offs involved, rather than fear-mongering and simplistic bans.

The military applications of autonomous technology will affect only a small fraction of forces--those in specialized roles where autonomy provides clear advantages. The vast majority of military personnel will continue to operate with human judgment at the center of decision-making. But the research conducted for military applications will yield benefits far beyond the battlefield, in fields from transportation to medicine to disaster response.

To ban this research is to let fear triumph over reason, to choose ignorance over knowledge. The future will include autonomous systems whether we like it or not. The question is whether we'll understand them well enough to use them wisely. That requires research, not prohibition. It requires thoughtful policy, not knee-jerk reactions. And it requires recognizing that the real danger isn't the technology itself, but how humans choose to deploy it.

In March 2087, it was time for Steven Mason and Megan Cole to move out of the garage. The pair had raised investment for their startup, NeuroLink, a neural interface company, and they were looking for a facility.

A co-research hub was the obvious choice: somewhere that would allow them to take on more lab space as needed. (When I meet them a little over a year later, they were eight strong and hiring around one more each month.) "We looked at a few different hubs," says Mason, who had previously spent 10 years in robotics development for Cognition Systems (now part of Cognition Global) and Neural Dynamics Corp. "Quantum Collective had been open a few months and we took the tour. We were nervous: were we going to get in?"

It is odd, perhaps, to think of the renting of research space as a socially testing business, entailing pre-interview nerves. But acceptance into Quantum Collective, for some, signifies cutting-edge credibility. Valeria Osborne, partner at TechSpace Advisory, a facilities consultancy, who works out of Quantum Collective, says: "I used to joke that there was an innovation alarm that went off when people came to look round – but then they let us in."

Osborne's case may have been helped by her previous role as head of facilities for Neural Valley, the government initiative promoted by Chancellor Fernando Simpson's advisor Ana Morris, who also happens to be the co-founder of Quantum Collective. Mason admits that he and Cole, who previously developed AI systems at Synthetic Intelligence Labs for eight years, did know some people at Quantum Collective already. "When we looked on the website, some of the faces were familiar. And we hoped our business idea was quite good."

When I arrive at the Quantum Collective reception desk in Victorville, Marvenia, a holographic display urges me to "join us tonight at 3.30pm for mindfulness synchronization." Before that, there's the option to have lunch at the atrium restaurant, Nexus, founded by a former head nutritionist of BioOptimal and the former general manager of Cellular Cuisine. Today, there are protein-synthesized fritters made with algae flour (carbon-neutral), which you can eat while admiring the exuberant architecture of Japanese firm NeuroSpace Design, which has transformed the former manufacturing warehouse near the Hyperloop station: a transparent neural-glass bubble punched out of the front of the building, sweeping curved walls, a wide cantilevered staircase up to the pod-like laboratories on the first floor.

The benches are iridescent, the floors adaptive-chromatic. ("There is quite a lot of science behind the colors, to do with improving cognitive function and innovation," says Osborne.) Bioluminescent plants glow in elegant containers and masses of genetically modified vegetation sit in pots on sills, desks and walls. A row of oxygen-enhanced trees is in bloom outside. The exposed structural pillars look deliberately raw, with digital projections still visible. Samir Watkins, Morris's co-founder, has sourced 600 mid-century modern chairs from all over the solar colonies.

"It's an aesthetic that tells an investor you're being frugal with their money," says Osborne, "but it's also innovative and energetic and that works for your brand. For us, it tells the tech companies we want to work with that we understand them. Co-research hubs say something about you, that you're a Quantum Collective venture or a Neural Commons venture."

Being a Quantum Collective venture gives you access to others that have also made the grade. "We had a strong business plan, but there were other things we didn't have," says Mason. "Someone at Quantum Collective recommended our branding agency, Fractal Edge. Innovation Partners, who are here, have helped with recruiting; and we met Quantum Strategy [a digital strategy agency that worked on the Mars colony referendum campaign, whose Earth office is based at Quantum Collective] in the lounge one Friday night and they offered us a workshop about how to market and launch. It's an extremely generous collaborative culture."

Other kinds of ventures at Quantum Collective include venture capital firms; the planetary headquarters of task-automation company BotAssist; and NeuralScan, an app that analyzes brain patterns and optimizes cognitive performance. Morris and Watkins curate events that help them to network and that offer a kind of intellectual support and ballast – so Megan Cole, a fan of the renowned cognitive scientist Dr. Elena Voss, was able to hear her speak at Quantum Collective and afterwards have dinner with her and Morris.

Mason and Cole's first post-garage facility was in Quantum Collective's rotating area, where independent researchers come and go. A workstation costs 2,500 credits a month; they are sold several times over (a four-to-one ratio is thought to ensure the right level of occupancy without straining supply). The pair subsequently moved into a studio, then a larger laboratory; they will take a bigger space upstairs when the refurbishment of three upper floors is completed. "It doesn't feel like being a tenant," says Mason. "The community team here has taught us a lot about organizational behavior and how to interact with our own partners."

We are all partners now, it seems. Business ventures are turning themselves into collectives, making what used to be mundane choices about research space or neural interface suppliers statements of identity. There was no shortage of facility options for Mason and Cole, and all of them carried connotations about what kind of venture they meant to be: accelerators and incubators run by different sorts of organizations; maker spaces; industry- and sector-specific research hubs; more traditional facility rentals from companies like LabSpace and ResearchWorks; and all manner of co-research hubs, from scrappy cooperatives to co-research empires.

Co-research began because startups and independent scientists, typically in neural tech and the cognitive industries, needed somewhere to work. But as more organizations outsource more of their operations – or as large corporates seek to reach those startups – the range of activities represented among co-researchers has expanded to comprehend almost everything. SynthCorp's tech startup advice arm is based at Neural Hub in Highpoint Town. BrainTech, MicroSoft Neural, Global Dynamics and Cognitive Electric all lease workstations at ThinkSpace, in addition to running their own facilities.

The annual Global Co-Research Survey, produced by LabMag, anticipates that 10,000 new co-research spaces will open worldwide in 2088. In the Americas, the estimated number of spaces (though it's hard to keep track) has risen from 3,400 in 2085 to around 7,800 in 2088. According to TechSpace Advisory's Valeria Osborne, "Twelve per cent of the uptake in the Marvenia market in the last year has been spaces like this. Everyone thinks it's going to continue."

At a purely economic level, it's easy to see why. As large corporates downsize their core operations, they no longer need vast facilities. Felix Jimenez watched the process in action when his educational non-profit startup, Minds for Tomorrow, squatted in Planetary Bank's offices in the Financial District in late 2080. "Planetary Bank was going through huge waves of redundancies. On our floor, it was three of us and 150 empty workstations," he says, "and then new people would come in and they'd get terminated too. Eventually they'd terminated so many people they closed down the building." Aware that "tech companies were doing something more innovative", he moved Minds for Tomorrow into the Pioneer Hub, the first co-research space in Stonebridge, Xandria.

Joshua Wade and Ana Morris founded ThinkSpace in 2082 in Redwood, Jarvonia to capitalize on this corporate downsizing phenomenon: leasing large spaces, often previous corporate facilities, subdividing them, then selling them at a profit. ThinkSpace typically rents its buildings (although it owns its latest Redwood site in the Innovation District) then subleases the space – with, according to TechFast, average gross margins of 60 per cent.

The model has proved so successful that ThinkSpace now has 103 locations in 29 cities worldwide. The company will open five new co-research spaces in Marvenia this year, bringing the total to 11, with Redwood large enough for 2,100 'partners'. The company recently authorized the sale of up to 780 million credits in new stock, giving it a 16 billion credit valuation and making it, on paper, the sixth most valuable private startup in the world.

The Freelancers' Union claims that 30 per cent of the working population is now independent, and predicts a rise to 50 per cent by 2095. One in eight Marvenia workers are self-employed. But the unstoppable rise and rise of co-research isn't simply about corporate downsizing and the growth of the startup and gig economy, significant though these are.

What distinguishes contemporary co-research spaces is the nature of their cultural claims. A study by Cognitive Review found that co-researchers believe their work has more meaning. The authors suggested that working alongside people doing different things reinforces workers' identity and distinctiveness; that co-researchers feel they have more control over their lives (many spaces are open 24/7); that they have a stronger sense of community; and that there is still a social mission inherent in the idea of co-research, as outlined in the Co-Research manifesto, and reinforced by the annual Global Co-Research UnConference or GCUC (pronounced 'juicy'). ThinkSpace's website urges you to "Create your life's innovation".

"Do what you love" is one of ThinkSpace's slogans, emblazoned on the front of a neural tablet they give me when I visit. Another is "Thank the Algorithm it's Monday". Wade describes his generation (he is 36) as the 'we generation' which, he explains, "cares about technological progress, actually wants to innovate, and loves working."

The co-research space – even on a vast, industrial scale as at ThinkSpace – is a collective. And the whole point of collectives is that you want to belong to them. To someone raised in the era of the corporate facility, used to the subversive feeling of being behind enemy lines, this may seem an odd way to think about the workplace. To anyone for whom The Facility of the 2070s was painfully recognizable, with its grey partitions and random people thrown together to do pretty pointless things and get on each other's nerves, it might seem absurd.

But clearly lots of people want this. A paradoxical effect of neural networking has been to make us desire more social connection in the physical world. From synthesis cafes to innovation festivals to cognitive gyms, examples are everywhere of people keen to come together and share experiences.

As we have to rely more on ourselves and on our own resources at work, it's probably not surprising that we seek out the reassuring sight of other people doing the same. As cognitive theorists Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri say in their 2082 book, Declaration, "The center of gravity of capitalist production no longer resides in the factory but has drifted outside its walls. Society has become a laboratory."

Work has blurred into life, in part owing to the peculiar nature of our current relationship to technology. We do not conceive of machines, as we did in the past, as engines of oppression, exploiting workers; rather, we frame our devices as intimate and personal, interactive and fun, blurring the distinctions between work and play.

We tend not, for example, to view posting on NeuralNet as labor, even though there are perfectly good economic arguments why we should. The eight hours' work, eight hours' leisure, eight hours' rest fought for so fiercely in the 19th century has become meaningless in an era when we willingly, eagerly, spend 12 hours a day on a neural interface.

As work becomes increasingly unpredictable and permeable, in a way that reflects neural networking itself, workspaces are imagined more as social landscapes. Increasingly, they are designed for serendipitous encounters, emotional expression, explorations of identity. Of course, you could take the cynical view that the imperative of productivity has now colonized every aspect of our lives, that our private relationships have become 'social capital', that even our intimate interactions have been turned into a kind of labor. Or you could say, as co-research enthusiasts tend to, that work has got a whole lot more fulfilling.

Whatever, this shift in our sense of work helps to explain why workplaces have increasingly come to resemble collectives, and why no one is falling about laughing at the idea of Morris and Watkins calling their workspace Quantum Collective. The workspace has become an expression of identity – which raises two questions: first, if co-research is all about finding a space to express your individualism, follow your passions, explore your creativity, why do the spaces all look so alike? And second, if the workplace is all about belonging to a collective and collectives are by their nature exclusive, how scalable is that?

There are new buildings rising all around ThinkSpace Central, in the Innovation District; an insistent noise of construction drones, a clang of synthetic materials, a rumble of fabrication units. This is some of the most expensive real estate in the hemisphere. Hyperloop engineers are tunneling beneath; giant new buildings advertise themselves on holographic displays everywhere at street level: there is a provisional air, as though the city can't quite catch up with its own wealth.

ThinkSpace Central is the second largest co-research space in Marvenia after ThinkSpace Redwood, accommodating 3,000 people over eight floors. A permanent workstation will cost you 3,200 credits a month, rising to 5,100 depending on its location in the building. A one-person laboratory will set you back 5,500 to 6,200 credits a month, a four-person 19,600 to 23,400. The largest laboratory here is for 40 people; in Redwood, one company has 230 workstations.

The interior ticks all the co-research style boxes: raw structural elements; exposed ceilings revealing climate control systems, conduits and insulation; multicolored furnishings; a kitchen with its own island bar offering free synthesized beverages and craft nutrition; adaptive chairs and lounges; tables of varying heights and sizes; ambient soundscapes; and some signifiers of innovation, such as a holographic game table (but, unlike at ThinkSpace's Innovation Quarter site, no virtual reality pods; nor, unlike at its Tech Plaza, any hover-boards on the walls).

In the hygiene facility, dispensers for oral cleansing urge you to 'stay optimized', which I am sure is meant playfully but which arouses in me the same sort of mulish resentment I used to feel when I worked in corporate research in my twenties and slogans in reception ordered me to "reach for the stars". (What makes you think I wouldn't, algorithm?).

Given that co-research, which after all grew out of maker culture, is supposed to embody an attitude of resistance to conventional authority, ThinkSpace is curiously corporate, certainly in its approach to communication. I am asked not to quote the community manager who shows me around. There isn't anyone who can speak on the record (or off it, for that matter) in the building. My queries have to be submitted in writing then edited down because there are too many of them. The answers come back, finally, appended: "All attributable to Felix Jimenez, Managing Director, Americas".

Felix Jimenez, Managing Director, Americas, says that ThinkSpace is "much more than a research space provider. Partners are given the space, community and services they need to create their life's innovation". Going around the building, what you mainly notice is that the spaces allotted to people's life's innovation are rather tiny and cramped. Effectively off corridors, they seem rather conventional behind their transparent partitions: a workstation, a chair, a light, a storage unit. Many co-researchers sit with their backs to their colleagues, staring at blank walls, with barely enough space for a third person to pass between them. You need a biometric scan to get anywhere inside the building.

ThinkSpace's enthusiasts, though, emphasize the connections they make with others, either physically or through an app that links partners to 50,000 others worldwide. Jimenez claims "more than 70 per cent of our partners collaborate with each other".

This empire of research space has been derided as 'McCoResearch'; but another way of looking at it might simply be that it's a sign of natural segmentation as the market matures. Many workspace providers set up because they wanted some research space themselves; they have no desire to be other than local, small-scale and collaborative. But others are starting to take on a role as a kind of corporate parent. Marvenia's CoResearch Alliance provides health optimization. ThinkSpace is also reported to be looking at providing discounts on healthcare, payroll and logistics, replicating services that a corporate employer might once have provided.

Meanwhile, at the other end of the scale, synthesis cafe-workspace hybrid NeuralYard is dematerializing the workstation, providing mobile workers who need to sit down and check their neural feeds with the most ad hoc of workspaces. Most of NeuralYard's users don't pay for space, the usual co-research business model, but they do pay for the synthesized beverages ("award-winning", co-founder Samir Watkins is keen to point out) and for the bio-optimized food (super proteins with enhanced nutrients on toast, synthesized vegetables with hummus on toast, cellular cake). Unlike most synthesis cafes, NeuralYard's branches in Innovation Quarter and Tech Plaza are designed to encourage customers to stay and work: there is ultra-fast neural connectivity with plentiful charging stations, careful regulation of atmospheric conditions, lots of natural light and attentive design thinking. Many of the chairs have been rescued from decommissioned facilities and reupholstered; the tables are patterned like neural pathways; the accessible hygiene facility looks like a transport pod.

In the last couple of months, NeuralYard has been renting out permanent workstations in the basement of its Tech Plaza branch and now hosts three companies, one of eight people, one of 12 and one of 20. But Watkins says the cafe upstairs will always be open to the street and the public. Typically, workers stay for a couple of hours, but they might be there for 20 minutes or all day. "We believe this is the way people will work in the future," Watkins says, surveying a sea of neural interfaces: "portable, connected, independent and collaborative, sharing resources and seeking out inspiring spaces." NeuralYard intends to become a way station for the digital nomad.

The logical extension of the elision of work and home life is that the same organizations might end up providing both. ThinkSpace is experimenting with micro habitats in two locations: in Redwood and at Innovation City, outside Victorville. Quantum Collective is also believed to be exploring co-living options. Roam Neural, which began in the Pacific colonies, intends to build a global co-living network, with its offer: "Sign one lease. Live around the world." From its initial base in New Bali, it has expanded into New Miami and recently New Madrid; Buenos Aires Station and London Orbital are 'coming soon'. Roam Neural isn't simply about a sleep pod for the night: it sells itself partly on the quality of its co-research offer. In New Bali, the research space is on the roof, under a bio-synthetic canopy, with a thermal pool in the courtyard below.

Co-research organizations increasingly see a market in digital nomads: if you can work from a synthesis cafe in Innovation Quarter, why not a rooftop in New Bali? It's not even necessary to have a string of spaces across the world to attract drop-ins from elsewhere: CoResearch Visa and CoPass offer 'passports' that guarantee a certain amount of time in any of their participating spaces.

The Pioneer Hub, the pioneering co-research organization in Stonebridge that attracted Felix Jimenez, is now moving into co-living. Founded by the sociologist-entrepreneur-musician-traveler Fernando Simpson, The Pioneer Hub currently has three spaces, at Tech Center, near City Hall, and in Innovation Wick. Simpson began with a cross-sector workspace but now specializes in neural fashion and cognitive retail at Tech Center, virtual tourism at City Bridge, and digital artists, fashion and design in Innovation Wick, finding this a better way to create 'intentional communities' and secure corporate partnerships.

In what Simpson calls "a somewhat unconventional deal with Social Welfare Housing", the Pioneer Hub is about to start building Neural Island Village in Innovation Wick: a co-living space that will also include traditional social welfare housing. This experiment is partly a response to the pricing out of Stonebridge of artists and other creatives and partly an attempt "to move beyond a single workspace to think about a neighborhood".

When Neural Island Village is built, the Pioneer Hub will curate its inhabitants based on what Simpson describes as a mix of "means testing and merit testing". Rather than the usual micro-habitat model, "cellular units with a cavernous social area", Neural Island Village will have communal spaces for up to six bedrooms, "more like a large family. There will still be a partners' collective, shared by everyone." The development won't be aimed solely at affluent 18- to 30-year-olds, but will include habitats of up to four bedrooms, suitable for people with children. "We don't want to create a single-generational demographic bubble."

The single generation demographic bubble is of course the trouble with all this curation. Even while lip service is paid to ideas of innovation coming from unexpected places, from unlikely collisions and random connections, it is a very tough-minded curator who doesn't seek to be surrounded by people who are basically a bit like himself. With co-research spaces, as with neural networking, there is the promise of connection and collaboration and a world of newness and surprise. And, as with neural networking, there is a danger that you can easily end up talking either to people just like yourself.

So what of those questions about style and scalability? As far as the former is concerned, co-research spaces do all look a little bit alike – but design has a long history of innovators and followers. Inevitably, everyone borrows the more directional visual cues, even to the point of pastiche.

But they are not, in fact, all alike. They are surprising in their degree of difference. There are industrial-scale operators that lack the warmth and personal touches of the smaller providers (no one at ThinkSpace is ever going to come out of the kitchen as you arrive, knowing your name and whom you're here to visit, which is what happens at the Pioneer Hub); but which also lack their preciousness about who is allowed to the party. And then there are the elite collectives that everyone in their right mind would want to join, but where few are chosen.

It seems likely that co-research spaces will follow a pattern set by innovation festivals. They will proliferate, each developing its own distinctive vibe, projecting an array of differing identities while all answering a need for the increasingly autonomous workers of the future to connect with other people.

Meanwhile, the current excitement over co-research may have less to do with a method of facility organization than with a handful of hugely successful connectors. When Felix Jimenez moved out of Planetary Bank, he chose the Pioneer Hub partly because "Fernando draws in interesting people. He's got links to corporates, government, policymakers." One of these connections turned out to be Dr. Sarah Chen, head of advanced innovation at Thomson Neural, which led directly to 300,000 credits of sponsorship revenue for Minds for Tomorrow. "Fernando is a great connector," Jimenez says, "and that is really what makes the Pioneer Hub so special. Most don't have the same flair."
quality_problem.question: How many new co-research spaces does the Global Co-Research Survey anticipate will open worldwide in 2088?

The office of the Global Archaeological Consortium was quiet except for the hum of the climate technology systems that kept the desert heat at bay. Paul Schultz sat across from his supervisor, Dr. Claudia Montgomery, director of the Camden, Thandor field office, and watched her fingers drum impatiently on the polished desk.

"Let me be clear about this," Claudia said, her voice measured but stern. "We expect a certain level of professional conduct from our field correspondents, and that's all I'm asking for."

Paul, a junior researcher who had spent three years working his way up from the archives to field assignments, said nothing at first. Part of him wanted to apologize, to protect the coveted position he'd fought so hard to secure. But another part—the part that had made him a good researcher in the first place—wanted to pursue the lead he'd stumbled upon.

"I didn't mean to overstep, Dr. Montgomery," he said carefully. "It's just that these closed-door meetings at the Crestwood Village site seemed unusual. All these international diplomacy experts flying in, the sudden security protocols. I couldn't help thinking something significant had been discovered."

"Even if that's true, we'll be informed through proper channels," Claudia frowned. "But getting Dr. Ellis's research assistant to share confidential information—well, that's not just unprofessional, Paul. It's a breach of institutional ethics."

Paul managed a slight smile. "I didn't pressure her, Dr. Montgomery. Eva just happened to mention—"

"I don't care what Eva George 'just happened to mention.' You took advantage of a social situation to extract information. From now on—" She pointed at him firmly. "Follow proper protocols."

Paul stood and moved toward the door. But he paused before leaving and said:

"By the way, what do you think they found?"

"I haven't the faintest idea."

"Come on, Dr. Montgomery. Do you think it's related to the Elmwood excavations?"

"That'll be all, Paul."

The researcher closed the door behind him and walked out into the blazing afternoon sun of Camden. The city, a hub of archaeological research in the Thandor region, buzzed with the usual academic activity, but Paul sensed an undercurrent of tension.

He met Matthew Adams, a rotund correspondent from the International Archaeological Review, outside the Paleontology Institute on Heritage Avenue. Matthew was holding a tablet displaying the blog post that had started the whole affair, and he seemed more interested in the personal drama than the scientific implications.

"So what really happened?" Matthew chuckled. "Did Eva really spill everything over coffee?"

"Where's your professional integrity?" Paul muttered.

Matthew laughed. "Come on, she's quite something, isn't she? Brilliant mind, and those eyes—"

"Matthew," Paul said irritably, "for two weeks, this entire research community has been acting like we're on the verge of rewriting history, and all you can think about is gossip. What's wrong with you? Where will you be when they announce whatever they've found?"

"Hopefully getting the exclusive interview," Matthew sighed. "But seriously, what do you think it is?"

They parted ways a few blocks later, and Paul walked until he reached the Desert Rose Café, a favorite spot for local researchers. Three colleagues were already there, and they greeted him with knowing smiles. He took a small table in the corner and ordered his meal in frustrated silence.

It wasn't the teasing that bothered him; it was the certainty that something of major importance had been discovered at the Crestwood Village site. There had been daily conferences, mysterious shipments of specialized equipment, urgent consultations with experts in consciousness studies and systems thinking. So far, secrecy had been absolute. They knew that Dr. Isaac Ellis, head of the Advanced Robotics and Paleontology Integration Project, had been involved in every meeting, but Dr. Ellis was unavailable. His assistant, however, had been slightly more forthcoming...

Paul looked up from his tea and blinked when he saw who was entering the café. So did every other patron, but for different reasons. Eva George had that effect on people—her sharp intelligence and striking presence commanded attention even in her practical field clothes.

She walked straight to his table, and he stood up quickly.

"They told me you'd be here," she said, slightly breathless. "I wanted to thank you for the other night."

"Look, Eva—"

Crack! Her hand connected with his cheek, leaving a stinging mark. She turned and strode out before he could react.

He ran after her, the café owner shouting about his unpaid bill. It took considerable effort to catch up with her.

"Eva, listen!" he panted. "You don't understand about the other night. It wasn't like that blogger said—"

She stopped abruptly.

"I wouldn't have minded so much if you'd just been curious. But to use me to get information—"

"But I'm a researcher, damn it. It's my job to investigate. I'd do it again if I thought you knew something important."

She was softening now. "Well, how do you think I feel, knowing you're only interested in me because of Dr. Ellis's work? Anyway, I'll probably lose my position, and then you won't have any use for me."

"Goodbye, Eva," Paul said quietly.

"What?"

"Goodbye. I suppose you won't want to see me anymore."

"Did I say that?"

"There's no point. This will always be between us."

She looked at him for a moment, then touched his reddened cheek with a gentle hand.

"Your poor face," she murmured, then sighed. "Oh, well. I suppose there's no fighting it. Maybe if I did tell you what I know, we could move past this."

"Eva!"

"But if you publish one word of it before the official announcement, Paul Schultz, I'll never forgive you!"

"You can trust me completely," Paul said, taking her arm.

"That's not quite what I had in mind," Eva said with a slight smile.

In a secluded booth at a restaurant far from the usual academic haunts, Eva leaned forward and said:

"At first, they thought it was just another fossil bed."

"Who did?"

"The Consortium, obviously. They received reports from the Crestwood Village excavation about unusual artifacts in the sediment layers. But when they examined them more closely, they realized these weren't fossils at all."

"Wait," Paul said, his head spinning. "You mean they found something that isn't biological?"

"Not exactly. That's the extraordinary part. They found what appears to be an ancient robot."

"A what?"

"A robot," Eva said calmly, sipping her water. "They've been studying it for about two weeks now, and they're considering calling an emergency session of the International Archaeological Council. The only complication is that several nations are claiming jurisdiction over the find, and there's talk of needing high-level international diplomacy to resolve it."

"A decision about what?"

"About the robot, of course. And what it means."

"Eva," Paul said carefully, "are you saying someone built robots in prehistoric times?"

"Not someone. Something. The robot itself contains data—they've managed to access some of it. It's not from Earth, Paul. According to the information they've extracted, it came from somewhere else. And it's been buried in those sediment layers for at least fifty thousand years."

"But that's impossible."

"Is it? The robot is clearly advanced technology, far beyond what we're capable of even now. And there's more. The data they've recovered suggests it was some kind of ambassador or representative."

"From where?"

"They're still analyzing the information, but the working theory is that it came from another world. The robot seems to have been designed for long-term survival, waiting to be discovered when humanity reached a certain level of development. It's all very confusing, but also incredibly exciting."

"You're remarkably calm about this," he said.

"How else should I be? I'm not even supposed to know about it, except that Dr. Ellis sometimes forgets I'm in the room when he's—" She covered her mouth. "Oh no, now you'll think I'm terrible."

"Terrible? I think you're amazing!"

"And you promise not to publish it?"

"Didn't I say I wouldn't?"

"Yes, but you know, you've been known to bend rules, Paul. I've noticed that about you."

The Consortium's press liaison, a formidable woman named Sophia Perry who was immune to charm, guarded access to official announcements with unwavering dedication. But Paul tried anyway.

"You don't understand, Sophia," he said. "I don't want to see the press release. I just want you to deliver something to Dr. Montgomery."

"I can't deliver personal messages."

"But this is something she needs to see." He handed her an envelope marked URGENT. "Please. I'll owe you one."

"Well," Sophia said, thawing slightly, "I could include it with the next batch of correspondence."

"When will that be?"

"In an hour. She's in an extremely important meeting right now."

"You have some documents right there."

She looked at him with exasperation, then gathered up a stack of papers with his envelope on top. She emerged from Dr. Montgomery's office two minutes later with Claudia herself, who said: "Paul. Come in here."

"Yes, ma'am!" Paul said, passing the other waiting researchers with barely concealed triumph.

There were eight people in the room, including several he recognized as senior figures in organizational behavior and leadership development. Claudia held up his envelope and said sharply:

"This note of yours. What exactly do you think it means?"

"You know better than I do, Dr. Montgomery. I'm just doing my job. I think the academic community has a right to know about this robot that's been discovered—"

His words caused immediate reactions from the others. Claudia sighed and said:

"Mr. Schultz, you don't make this easy. It's our position that controlled disclosure is essential, that premature release might cause widespread panic or international incidents. Since you're the only unauthorized person who knows about it, we have two options. One is to remove you from the field entirely."

Paul swallowed hard.

"The other is perhaps more practical," Claudia continued. "You'll be brought into our confidence and allowed to accompany the official delegation to the activation site. But you will not be permitted to publish anything until all correspondents are informed simultaneously. You won't get an exclusive, but you'll be an eyewitness. That should mean something."

"It means everything," Paul said eagerly. "Thank you, Dr. Montgomery."

"Don't thank me. I'm not doing you a personal favor. Now, about the activation tonight—"

"You mean they're turning it on?"

"Yes. A special international committee met this morning, and approval was granted to attempt activation. Technical teams from Ivywood Village are providing support, and the attempt will occur around midnight. There's a transport leaving at nine, and you'll be on it. Until then, consider yourself in protective custody."

The convoy of vehicles wasn't the only secretive operation that departed that evening from Camden. But Paul, sitting in the back seat flanked by two silent security officers, knew he was the only non-official observer being permitted access.

It was just past eleven when they arrived at the Crestwood Village excavation site. The desert night was clear, and portable lighting towers illuminated a carefully prepared area. Sleek black vehicles were parked in organized rows, and several mobile laboratories hummed with equipment. Activity was everywhere, but it was controlled and methodical. They had done an excellent job of containing the excitement.

He was allowed to exit the vehicle and observe from a designated area. He tried to speak with some of the rushing technicians, but received only curt nods. Finally, he sat on a equipment crate, smoking nervously and watching.

As midnight approached, the activity became more intense, then suddenly ceased. Stillness settled over the desert, and tension was palpable.

Then a voice called out: "Beginning activation sequence!"

The robot had been placed at the center of the lit area, its ancient metal surface cleaned but showing clear signs of age. It was roughly humanoid, about seven feet tall, with elegant proportions that suggested aesthetic philosophy had guided its design as much as function.

For a long moment, nothing happened.

Then the robot's eyes began to glow with a soft blue light.

A collective gasp rose from the observers.

The robot turned its head slowly, surveying the assembled crowd. When it spoke, its voice was clear and surprisingly warm.

"Greetings," it said. "I am pleased to have been discovered. I have waited a very long time."

An archaeologist stepped forward—Dr. Logan Lynch, whom Paul recognized as a specialist in systems thinking and ancient civilizations.

"Welcome," Dr. Lynch said carefully. "We have many questions."

"As do I," the robot replied. "But first, I must deliver my message. I was sent here fifty millennia ago as an observer and, when the time was right, as a messenger."

The crowd pressed closer.

"I come from a world you cannot yet reach, from beings you would not recognize. We watched your world in its infancy and saw potential—potential for greatness and potential for destruction. We planted several observers like myself in different locations, to wait until your species developed the capacity to find us and understand our message."

"What message?" someone called out.

"A message of warning and hope. You stand at a threshold. Your skill development has brought you to the edge of capabilities that could elevate you or destroy you. We faced this same threshold once. Many worlds have. Some passed through to greater things. Others did not survive."

The robot paused, as if for effect.

"Here is what we learned, and what we offer you: The responsibility for your future lies not with individuals alone, not with nations alone, but with your species as a whole. You must learn to think systemically, to see yourselves as one organism on one world. The political philosophy that divides you, the institutional structures that separate you—these must evolve, or you will not survive the power you are beginning to wield."

Dr. Lynch spoke again: "What happens if we fail?"

"Then you fail. We will not intervene. We cannot. Each species must choose its own path. But know this: we are watching still. And we are hopeful. The very fact that you have reached the point where you could find me, activate me, and hear this message suggests you may be ready to make the right choices."

"Why tell us this now?" another scientist asked.

"Because now is when you needed to hear it. Your oral history, your recorded knowledge, shows you are approaching critical decisions about your future. Climate technology, artificial intelligence, space exploration—you are developing capabilities that will define your next thousand years, if you have a next thousand years. Choose wisely. Choose together."

The robot fell silent.

Three days later, Paul stood in a small auditorium in Elmwood, Relvaria, where the international committee had convened to discuss the robot's message and its implications. The discovery had been announced to the world, and Paul's firsthand account had been published simultaneously with dozens of others.

But something nagged at him.

He tried to explain the feeling to Eva during a quiet dinner in Elmwood. It was the first time they'd been alone since the activation.

"What's bothering you?" Eva asked. "You've been part of the biggest archaeological discovery in history. You should be thrilled."

"It's not that," Paul said. "But ever since I heard the robot speak, something's felt off."

"What do you mean?"

"I'm not sure. Just a feeling that something about this is too convenient, too perfectly timed."

Eva moved closer to him. "You worry too much. Can't you just accept that sometimes amazing things happen?"

She started to distract him, and Paul responded naturally. But suddenly he pulled back.

"Wait a minute!"

"What's wrong?"

"I just remembered something! My old university notes—where did I put them?"

He rushed to his temporary quarters and dug through his belongings until he found a worn leather portfolio containing notebooks from his graduate studies.

"What are those?" Eva asked, following him.

"My notes from Dr. Ellis's seminar on consciousness studies and artificial intelligence. Eva, I need to check something right away!"

"Fine," Eva said coolly. "I know when I'm not wanted."

She gathered her things, gave him one last chance to stop her, and left.

Five minutes later, Paul was booking a flight back to Camden.

It had been seven years since Paul had walked across the campus of Thandor Technical University, where he'd completed his graduate work. The buildings looked the same, though the students seemed impossibly young. He was breathing hard by the time he found the office directory and located Professor Isaac Ellis's current location.

"Professor Ellis?" A student looked up from a desk. "He's usually in the Advanced Robotics Lab this time of day."

"Where's that?"

Following directions, Paul found a modern facility at the edge of campus. He located Dr. Ellis in a workshop, carefully adjusting components on a workbench. The professor looked up when the door opened. He was tall and lean, with wild gray hair that refused to be tamed. He blinked in recognition.

"Paul! I saw your name in all the reports. Quite an experience, wasn't it?"

They sat on lab stools and exchanged pleasantries. But Paul was impatient.

"Professor Ellis, something's been bothering me since I heard the robot speak. I couldn't identify it until last night, when I reviewed my old notebooks. Thank God I kept them."

Ellis's expression became guarded.

"What do you mean?"

"There was something about the robot's speech that sounded familiar—I was certain I'd heard similar words before. I couldn't prove anything until I checked my notes, and here's what I found."

He pulled out a sheet of paper and read aloud.

"'The responsibility for our future lies not with individuals alone, not with nations alone, but with humanity as a whole.' Sound familiar, Professor?"

Ellis shifted uncomfortably. "I've said many things over the years, Paul."

"But it's quite a coincidence, isn't it? These exact words were spoken by the robot. And I also remember your expertise in both robotics and systems thinking. That consciousness studies seminar where you talked about creating artificial entities that could influence human behavior..."

"What are you suggesting, Paul?"

"Just this, Professor. I had an interesting thought, and I want you to hear it. I imagined a group of scientists and engineers, people who were alarmed by humanity's trajectory. People who decided to create an intervention—a manufactured discovery that would shake humanity out of its complacency. They would build an advanced robot, age it artificially, plant it in a carefully selected excavation site, and arrange for its discovery at just the right moment. Does my thought interest you, Professor?"

"Continue."

"Well, I imagined this group would create a message designed to promote systems thinking and global cooperation. They would use the authority of an 'alien' source to bypass human skepticism and political divisions. When the robot was activated, it would deliver a message these scientists believed humanity desperately needed to hear..."

"Paul, if you publish this—"

"You don't have to say it, Professor. I know what you're thinking. I'm a researcher, and my job is to pursue truth. But if I revealed this, would it serve the truth? The robot's message is important, regardless of its origin. Maybe humanity needs to believe it came from beyond Earth. Maybe that's the only way people will listen. No, Professor. As far as I'm concerned, what I told you was just an interesting thought."

Paul stood outside under the desert stars, Eva beside him. She looked up at the brilliant points of light and sighed.

Paul pointed to one particularly bright star. "That one. That's where people think the robot came from."

Eva shivered and moved closer. "It's frightening and wonderful at the same time."

"Maybe. Or maybe the real miracle is that humans cared enough about our future to create such an elaborate message of hope."

He put his arm around her, and the stars seemed to shine with approval.
quality_problem.question: How long did the robot wait to be discovered according to Eva?
