quality_problem.story:
The letter from the Fairview District Council arrived on a Tuesday morning, and I read it twice over breakfast before sharing it with my wife, Elena.

"What would you think," I asked her over tea, "if I should undertake to mentor a youth collective this autumn?"

She considered it while she cleared the breakfast dishes. "Why, Marcus," she said, "it could be quite enriching, if I understand what a youth collective entails. What prompted this?"

"It wasn't entirely my idea," I admitted. "Councilor Brennan called me to her office yesterday. She said that some of the younger citizens in the district wanted to establish one. They need adult guidance, of course, and one of them suggested my name."

I should explain that I teach courses in aesthetic philosophy and systems thinking at our Fairview Academy. It's a privilege to work in Fairview, for our institution values interdisciplinary approaches and encourages students to see connections between art, nature, and social organization. On the other hand, most of my students come from families deeply involved in the district's experimental governance projects, and there's a constant pressure to demonstrate practical applications of theoretical concepts.

"That's wonderful," said Elena. "What does a youth collective do?"

"The purpose," I told her, "is to teach young people about organizational behavior and collaborative decision-making. They identify community needs and develop creative solutions—sometimes artistic, sometimes practical. Some collectives have even influenced local trade policy."

"You won't have to go door-to-door selling things, will you?"

"Of course not. I'd just facilitate their process."

Elena laughed, and I joined her, for we both knew that my understanding of market economics was theoretical at best.

"All right," I said, "laugh at my practical limitations. But don't worry. Councilor Brennan said we could consult with Dr. Park from the Systems Department if needed. There is one consideration, though. The Council will provide two hundred credits for initial materials, and Brennan suggested I might contribute another hundred. The question is, can we manage it?"

We'd been careful with finances since moving to Fairview three years ago. Our previous home in Goldfield Town had been comfortable, but when the environmental crisis forced mass relocations, we'd had to start over. Fairview's experimental social contract appealed to us—a community built on principles of environmental ethics and collective governance—but it meant financial sacrifices.

Elena did quick calculations. "Yes," she said, "if it's something meaningful to you."

Three weeks later, on a crisp autumn morning, I found myself in a converted greenhouse at the edge of the district. This would serve as our workspace—a bright, plant-filled structure owned by the family of one of the collective members, Mateo Lawrence.

"All right," I said to the five young people arranged on cushions around a low table, "let's begin informally. I'm not here as your teacher. My role is simply to facilitate. You'll decide what the collective pursues, and if it aligns with our community values and available resources, I'll support it however I can. This is your gathering."

Councilor Brennan had briefed me extensively on these young people. The three sitting to my left had initiated the proposal.

Rita Hayes was a thoughtful twelve-year-old who might have seemed reserved to strangers, but possessed a remarkable intensity when discussing ideas. Wei Mason and Layla Hamilton, also twelve, shared Rita's careful way of speaking and moving. The three had been friends since early childhood.

I initially thought they looked similar, but this was misleading. Their features were quite distinct. Perhaps from years of close friendship, they'd developed similar patterns of gesture and expression. All three had been deeply tanned by summer sun, making their eyes seem luminous.

The two sitting to my right were different in temperament. Alice Cruz was a robust thirteen-year-old with abundant dark curls and an infectious enthusiasm. Mateo Lawrence, a few months younger, was energetic and outgoing, always ready with questions.

The group exchanged glances, and Wei seemed to be designated speaker.

"Well, Mr. Reyes, a youth collective is a group of young people who collaborate to address community needs, using systems thinking and creative approaches."

"Is that your goal?" I asked. "To address community needs?"

"Why not?" Mateo responded. "There's something wrong with trying to help?"

"We want to make a difference," said Layla. "And learn skills we'll need for future projects."

"What sort of projects interest you?" I asked.

Councilor Brennan had mentioned that these young people were exceptional. "Alice and Mateo," she'd said, "show remarkable aptitude for systems thinking—they see connections others miss. The other three are harder to categorize. They demonstrate extraordinary insight in certain areas, but often seem disengaged from standard curricula. Perhaps this collective will channel their abilities."

Alice said, "What about creating a community art installation? Something that changes with the seasons."

"We should map community needs first," Mateo suggested, "then design solutions."

"I'd like to work on natural resource management," said Wei. He fixed me with a challenging look. "We could develop a system for monitoring water usage patterns across the district."

"That would require sophisticated data science capabilities," I told him, "which might be beyond our current scope. Perhaps something more accessible?"

Wei considered this and nodded reluctantly. "Then maybe something involving aesthetic philosophy. A public art project that teaches environmental concepts."

"How about a community garden design?" Layla offered.

"You mean just landscaping?" I asked.

She looked slightly offended. "No, I mean applying principles of cultural evolution to plant selection. Creating a garden that demonstrates how human aesthetic preferences have shaped agricultural biodiversity. I've been researching this."

"Well," I said, "that sounds like it requires substantial botanical knowledge. Are you Dr. Hamilton's daughter? Been exploring your father's library?"

"Some," said Layla, "and I maintain experimental plots at home."

"What about you, Rita?" I prompted. "Do you have a particular interest?"

"I'm not specialized," she said with a slight smile. "More integrative. But if the collective wanted to document local bird populations, I could contribute data I've been collecting."

"You could make that useful?" Mateo asked skeptically.

"Bird populations," I explained to Mateo, "are important indicators of environmental health. Systematic observation of local species could provide valuable data. The district's environmental monitoring program might be interested."

"No," said Rita, "these aren't standard observations. I've been tracking behavioral changes in urban-adapted species. How they've modified nesting patterns in response to our building designs."

"Well," I admitted, "the application for that might be limited. Why don't you consider something more straightforward? Perhaps designing informational materials about the district's recycling program?"

There was a pause, then Mateo said, "How would we distribute them?"

"Door-to-door, or at community centers."

He made a face. "Limited impact. Unless the materials themselves demonstrated something. What if we made them from recycled materials in an unusual way—showing the potential?"

Layla had been deep in thought. She said suddenly, "I think I know how to make a living wall system—vertical gardens for apartment buildings."

"What would that involve?" I asked.

"Modular planters that connect to greywater recycling. Self-sustaining."

"There might be people interested in that," I conceded.

"There will be," she said confidently.

Mrs. Lawrence appeared after a while, bringing refreshments and asking about our progress. I'd forgotten entirely about organizational structure, which according to everything I'd read was essential. Standard practice was for each member to take a leadership role.

Over lunch, I suggested establishing roles, but they seemed uninterested. Wei waved it off, saying they'd work organically. They did spend considerable time discussing a name, finally settling on "Fairview Futures."

It was Alice who eventually suggested wind sculptures. At first there was mild interest, then Wei said, "We could design something new. Has anyone seen a wind sculpture that incorporates sound?"

Nobody had. Wei sketched in the air. "Hollow tubes of varying lengths, arranged to catch wind from multiple directions."

"I'll prototype something tonight," said Rita, "and work out the acoustics."

I wished they weren't starting with an invention, risking disappointment, but I said nothing, knowing I could help them adjust later.

That evening I told Elena about the day's ideas. Most seemed impractical, but several were intriguing.

Mateo wanted to create a game-theory-based simulation for teaching resource allocation—a board game that demonstrated tragedy of the commons scenarios.

Wei wanted to design modular furniture that could be reconfigured for different community gathering needs.

Layla, moving past her garden ideas, suggested creating seed packets with embedded information—QR codes that linked to growing guides and environmental impact data.

Rita added that if you designed the packets creatively, they could become collectible art objects, encouraging seed saving.

These ideas incorporated sophisticated concepts, and I spent some time discussing systems thinking principles with them.

"My," said Elena, "they're remarkably insightful. Mateo sounds like a natural facilitator. I don't think you'll need Dr. Park's help."

I feel somewhat embarrassed about the wind sculpture, even now. That it worked surprised me. That it worked so beautifully was humbling.

Four of them were at the greenhouse when I arrived the next morning, and the sculpture hung from a tree branch, its tubes singing softly in the breeze. I stood listening, then they noticed me.

"Hello, Mr. Reyes," Alice said, gesturing toward it. I examined the sculpture for several minutes. It was exquisitely crafted, with a professional quality.

"It's too perfect," Alice told Rita. "Art should have some rawness."

"You're right," Rita agreed. She adjusted one tube slightly. "There, now it has dissonance."

Indeed, in the morning breeze, the sculpture now produced an intriguing mix of harmony and tension.

As we walked back to the greenhouse, I asked Rita, "How did you know that angle would create dissonance?"

She looked thoughtful. "It had to, didn't it? It changed the resonance patterns." She glanced at me quickly. "Of course, I tried various configurations while building it."

"Naturally," I said. "Where's Mateo?"

"He went to the Council office," Wei told me, "to request funding. We'll need materials to produce more sculptures."

"But I said yesterday that Councilor Brennan and I were providing initial capital."

"Oh, certainly, but wouldn't it be better to go through official channels? More aligned with community values?"

"Perhaps," I said, "but the Council generally requires detailed proposals."

Mateo walked in and handed me a document. "I got five hundred credits approved. It took some discussion—half the environmental committee wanted to hear the proposal. The account's in your name, Mr. Reyes, and you'll need to authorize expenditures. They want you to stop by and sign the agreement."

My heart sank. I'd never dealt with bureaucratic funding processes, and they made me anxious. To say nothing of being responsible for five hundred credits. I mentally vowed to be very careful.

"So then I stopped by the arts supply cooperative," Mateo continued, "and ordered materials. We hadn't finalized a name yesterday, but I made an executive decision. Fairview Futures—how's that?"

Everyone nodded approval.

"Just simple design on the letterhead," he explained. "Fairview Futures—Highpoint, Yendor."

I found my voice. "Professionally printed, I assume?"

"Well, of course," he replied. "Presentation matters."

My appetite was subdued that evening, and Elena noticed my preoccupation, but asked no questions. I told her about the sculpture's success and the group's ambitious plans.

On Friday we established a production process, soon developing an efficient workflow: cutting tubes to calculated lengths, treating them with weatherproofing solution, assembling them in Rita's designed configurations, and hanging the finished sculptures to cure.

Wei had located a supplier of bamboo tubes, which produced wonderful tones and aligned with our environmental ethics. I didn't know what they cost until later.

Within two weeks we had nearly fifty sculptures completed and packaged. Frankly, I was ready for a break, but Mateo, our acknowledged expert on community engagement, wanted more inventory. This quantity satisfied him, and he said he'd begin outreach the following week.

Alice, with touching confidence, asked him to reserve one for her family.

Three other developments occurred that day. Alice brought her laptop and spent the afternoon working on what appeared to be quite competent graphic design for promotional materials.

And Layla brought samples of her seed packet designs. They were beautiful—small envelopes with botanical illustrations and embedded information chips.

"What species?" I asked.

Layla smiled. "Heritage vegetables adapted to our climate. I've been selecting for drought tolerance while maintaining flavor profiles."

"That's remarkable. How long have you been working on this?"

"Three growing seasons. I've documented everything—it's proper peer review quality data."

"Is it effective?"

She pulled out her phone and showed me growth comparison charts. "These varieties use 40% less water than commercial equivalents."

The third Friday development reached me on Monday morning.

I arrived at the greenhouse slightly late to find several vehicles parked outside and the space full of people, including two Council representatives. Our Fairview officials are quite young and informal, but they still looked official, though currently they were laughing.

"Well," I said in my best classroom voice, "what's happening here?"

"Are you Reyes?" the taller representative asked.

"I am," I said, and someone took a photograph.

A young journalist grasped my arm. "Oh, Mr. Reyes, please, tell me about the collective's work. This is exactly the kind of story we need."

"Perhaps someone should brief me first."

"You don't know? One of your members installed a wind sculpture in Stonegate's central plaza last night—without permission. It's wonderful, but it's caused quite a discussion about public art and the social contract."

I shook my head, stunned.

"It was perfect timing. Morning commuters discovered it, and by noon there was a crowd. The sculpture's song changes with the wind, and people are calling it 'The Voice of Stonegate.' And this morning"—she smiled—"someone anonymously contacted the Council—of course it was the same young person who installed it—Mateo?—and here we are. And we've just seen demonstrations of those amazing seed packets and heard the plans for vertical gardens."

"Gardens?"

"Yes, those modular living walls. Who would have thought young people could develop such sophisticated systems?"

After things settled, Mr. Lawrence came down from the house to see what the excitement was about, then returned to work. Mrs. Lawrence went back inside. The journalist and photographer left. Mateo was jubilant.

"Did you hear? They're calling it 'The Voice of Stonegate.' I wish we had a hundred sculptures ready. A thousand. This is exactly what community engagement looks like. Layla, how soon can you produce more seed packets? And Rita, how many bird behavior datasets do you have?"

Those datasets! I've always found ornithology interesting in theory, but I must admit Rita's work was genuinely impressive.

"How many observation hours?" I asked.

"About four hundred, across three years. Want to see the analysis?"

I won't try to explain her methodology, but it was clear she'd done rigorous systematic observation. We asked Mrs. Lawrence to join us for a discussion. She listened carefully.

"All right," she finally said, "if you're serious about this. But you'll need proper protocols for any research involving living creatures. And you can't use this greenhouse once winter comes—you'll need heated space."

"We'll have transitioned by then," Rita predicted. "Once our work is published, other researchers will replicate it. The collective will move on to new projects."

Rita was right, despite our concerns about scaling too quickly. After the
Fairview Chronicle
gave us most of page two, including photographs, we had regular visitors. Many wanted to purchase sculptures or seed packets, but Mateo insisted on working through established community channels.

The arts cooperative took all our sculptures at forty credits each—Mateo's pricing alarmed me, but they sold immediately. He valued the seed packets at fifteen credits per set and found ready buyers.

Our beautiful letterhead arrived, along with quickly printed project proposal forms.

The following Tuesday, a energetic woman extricated herself from her vehicle and walked into the greenhouse. I looked up from where I was assembling planter frames.

"Hi," she said. "You're Marcus Reyes, correct? I'm Dr. Sarah Kim, and I work in the intellectual property section at the district's innovation center. My supervisor sent me, though I'd have come anyway. What are you doing to protect Fairview Futures' innovations?"

I straightened up and brushed off my hands. "Well, I've been wondering about that, but I know very little about such matters—"

"Exactly," she interrupted. "We thought that might be the case. Three of us at the center would like to contribute time. Partly because we're interested, partly because you may have genuinely novel approaches worth protecting. Interested? You handle filing fees—about a hundred credits per innovation. We'll handle everything else."

"What's to lose," Mateo interjected.

And so we acquired intellectual property support.

The day our design application was filed, Alice contacted a dozen sustainable design firms, sent specifications to each, and offered licensing arrangements. Result: one licensee with a two-thousand-credit advance.

It was a foggy morning about three weeks later when I arrived at the greenhouse. Dr. Kim was there, along with everyone except Mateo. Sarah had her feet up on a work table.

"Hi," she said. "Good news."

"Tell me," I replied.

"I am," she said, "in a cautious legal sense, of course. Layla and I have been reviewing her seed development work. I've spent recent evenings studying agricultural patents and genetic selection literature. There are countless patents on crop varieties and selection methods, but it looks"—she held up a cautionary hand—"it just looks like we have something genuinely novel. If we get protection, you have a valuable property."

"That's good, Dr. Kim," Layla said, "but it's not the most important thing."

"No?" Sarah raised an eyebrow at me, and I handed her a small packet.

She opened it carefully. "What is this?"

"Soil amendment," Layla told her. "It's designed for Fairview's specific soil conditions. Try a bit."

Sarah examined it closely. "It's remarkably fine-textured, and there's something unusual about the color."

"It contains biochar and mycorrhizal fungi in a specific ratio. It improves water retention by 60% while enhancing nutrient availability."

"I see. What's in it?"

"Several components. Applied systems thinking. Waste wood from district maintenance, processed with controlled pyrolysis, combined with cultivated fungal cultures."

"Just several components. And does it work long-term?"

"Three growing seasons of data confirm it," I said.

Dr. Kim stood and looked out into the fog. After a moment she said, "Reyes, Layla and I are heading to my office. We can work better there, and if we're going to revolutionize urban agriculture, no time like the present."

After they left, I turned to the others. "Let's talk. Where's Mateo?"

"Oh, he went to the Council to request expanded funding."

"Whatever for? We have over eight thousand credits in the account."

"Well," Wei said, looking slightly sheepish, "we were planning to acquire some fabrication equipment. You see, Rita refined my idea for modular furniture." He grabbed paper. "Look, we make components that can be reconfigured using magnetic connections, like this—" And he was off explaining.

"What did they do today, dear?" Elena asked over dinner.

"Let's see. We selected fabrication equipment, Rita shared chapters from her book on urban ecology, and we found a space in the Fairview Arts Building we can rent for winter. Oh, and Sarah is starting the incorporation process."

"Winter space," Elena repeated. "You mean you're continuing after school starts?"

"Why not? The young people can manage their studies easily, and they'll only work a few hours weekly during the school year."

"Even so, isn't this a lot of responsibility for children?"

"They're not working for anyone. They're the collective. Dr. Kim and I will be the only formal staff—initially, anyway."

Elena looked startled. "Did you say you'd be staff?"

"Sure," I told her. "They've offered me a small stake in the collective, and I'd be foolish to refuse. After all, what's to lose?"
quality_problem.question: What is the name of the youth member whose family owns the greenhouse where meetings are held?

quality_problem.story:
The Salvage Run
By MARCUS CHEN

Stand by for the
M.S. Prometheus
, laughingstock of the Merchant Marine. She's got something revolutionary in her engines, and only her brilliant engineer can make it work!

Captain Samuel Perkins stood in the acidic rain of Forestdale Station, Belvoria, and stared at his new assignment with barely concealed disgust. The rain here never stopped—a consequence of the atmospheric processors that had made this moon habitable but had never quite gotten the weather right. Now a thick fog was rolling in from the industrial sectors, reducing visibility to near zero. It was a typical day on Belvoria.

Samuel cursed Administrator Chen and all his bureaucratic ancestors with considerable feeling. Then he motioned to his companion, and together they trudged through the muck toward the ancient cargo hauler.

The bulky frame of the Merchant Ship
Prometheus
loomed unhappily into the thick air above the two men as they reached the loading bay. Samuel raised reluctant eyes to the scarred hull of the fat cargo ship.

"It looks," he commented bitterly, "like a flying warehouse that lost a fight with an asteroid."

First Officer Anil Hunt—"Hunt" to his friends—nodded in agreement. "That's our Fire-Bringer... old Prommy herself. The ship with the cursed reputation." Hunt had been with her a full year, which was a record for First Officers on the
Prometheus
. She generally sent them back to Earth with stress disorders in half that time.

"Tell me, Captain," continued Hunt curiously, "how does it happen that you of all people happened to draw this tub for a command? I thought..."

"You know Chen?" queried Samuel.

Hunt nodded. "Oh, yes. Yes, indeed. Old Iron-Desk Chen?"

"The same."

"Well," Hunt ran a hand over his chin speculatively, "I know Chen's a prize bureaucrat... but you were in command of the
Constellation
. And, after all, you come from an old merchant family and all that. How come this?" He indicated the cargo hauler expressively.

Samuel sighed. "Well, now, Hunt, I'll tell you. You'll be shipping with me and I guess you've a right to know the worst... not that you wouldn't find it out anyway. I come from a long line of very successful captains. Five generations of officers and entrepreneurs. Steeped in tradition.

"The first Samuel Perkins, son of a shipping magnate, emerged from the Corporate Wars a fleet commander and Innovation Medal winner. Then came Samuel Perkins II, and in the Media Consolidation Crisis of 2087, he won a Transparency Citation for exposing corporate corruption. And then came Samuel Perkins III... me.

"From such humble beginnings do great traditions grow. But something happened when I came into the picture. I don't fit with the rest of them. Call it luck or temperament or what have you.

"In the first place, I seem to have an uncanny talent for saying the wrong thing to the wrong person. Chen for example. And I take too much initiative. Chen doesn't like that. I lost the
Constellation
because I left my assigned route to rescue a group of miners I thought were in danger from pollution control failures at an orbital refinery..."

"The Queenstown incident?" asked Hunt.

"So you've heard about it." Samuel shook his head sadly. "My environmental specialist warned me that the refinery's containment systems might fail catastrophically. I left my scheduled delivery to evacuate miners." He shrugged. "Wrong guess. No failure. I made an ass of myself and lost the
Constellation
. Chen gave it to his former protégé. I got this."

Hunt coughed slightly. "I heard something about Summit Station, too."

"Me again. The
Constellation's
whole crew ended up in the Ulvaria detention center. We celebrated a successful run a bit too freely."

Hunt looked admiringly at his new Commander. "That was the day after the
Constellation
broke the record for the Jarvonia-to-Belvoria run, wasn't it? And then wasn't there something about..."

"Springfield?"

Hunt nodded.

"That time I called the Trade Minister's economic policies 'a masterclass in how to destroy labor relations.' It was at a political economy summit."

"I begin to see what you mean, Captain."

"Samuel's the name, Hunt."

Hunt's smile was expansive. "Samuel, I think you're going to like our old rust bucket here." He patted the
Prometheus's
loading bay affectionately. "She's old... but she's independent. And we're not likely to meet any Ministers or Administrators with her, either."

Samuel sighed, still thinking of his sleek
Constellation
. "She'll haul cargo, I suppose. And that's about all that's expected of her."

Hunt shrugged philosophically. "Better than processing waste materials, anyway. Deep space?"

Samuel shook his head. "Belvoria-Selvoria."

Hunt scratched his chin speculatively. "Inner system run. Routine work."

Samuel was again looking at the ship's unprepossessing exterior. "A quantum-drive hauler, so help me."

Hunt nodded agreement. "The last of her class."

And she was not an inspiring sight. The unfortunately named
Prometheus
was a quantum-drive cargo hauler built some fifteen years back in the period immediately preceding the Resource Wars. She had been designed primarily for conventional cargo runs, with a quantum-drive system for emergency high-speed transport. At least that was the designer's vision. In those days, quantum propulsion was in its experimental stage, and at the time of the
Prometheus's
launching, the quantum-drive was hailed as the future of shipping.

Her designer, Marcus Schultz, had been awarded a Pioneer's Medal for her, and every shipping executive in the fleet had dreamed of commanding one of her class. There had been three. The
Atlas
, the
Titan
, and the prototype... old Prommy. The three vessels had gone into service during the Resource Crisis after the Selvoria Embargo had disrupted trade routes.

All three were spectacular failures.

The eager captains commanding the three haulers had found the quantum-drive too tempting not to use. They activated it... improperly.

The
Atlas
suffered a catastrophic engine failure. The
Titan
vanished in the general direction of the outer colonies, her quantum core destabilizing and creating a radiation hazard. And the
Prometheus's
port engines blew, causing her to spin uncontrollably under extreme acceleration until all her cargo and much of her interior equipment was destroyed, along with half her crew.

The
Prometheus
was refitted for service. And because it was an integral part of her design, the quantum-drive was rebuilt... and locked down. She became a workhorse, growing more temperamental with each passing year. She carried supplies. She hauled ore. She transported equipment and personnel. Now, she would carry time-sensitive medical supplies and research materials. She would lift from Forestdale and burn to Queenstown, Selvoria, without delay or variation. Regulations, tradition, and Administrator Chen of the Inner System Trade Authority required it. And it was now up to Samuel Perkins III to see to it that she did...

The Officer of the Deck, a sharp-featured woman in crisp uniform, saluted smartly as Samuel and Hunt stepped through the airlock.

Samuel felt vaguely uncomfortable. He knew, of course, that at least half the personnel on board civilian vessels was female, but he had never actually had women in senior positions on a ship of his own, and he felt quite certain that he preferred a different arrangement.

Hunt sensed his discomfort. "That was Rita Jenkins, Samuel. Lieutenant. Navigation Officer. She's excellent, too."

Samuel shook his head. "Don't like mixing professional and personal dynamics. Makes me uncomfortable."

Hunt shrugged. "Rita's the only senior officer. But about a third of our crew is female." He grinned maliciously. "Equal opportunity, you know."

"No doubt," commented the other sourly. "Is that why they named this... ship 'Prometheus'?"

Hunt saw fit to consider the question rhetorical and remained silent.

Samuel ducked through the hatchway to the main control deck. Hunt followed. He trailed his Captain through a maze of conduits and control panels to the main engineering station. Samuel sank into a command chair in front of the red LOCKED seal on the quantum-drive control.

"Looks like something from a particle physics lab, doesn't it?" commented Hunt.

Samuel nodded sadly, thinking of the streamlined efficiency of the
Constellation's
bridge. "But she's home to us, anyway."

The thick Belvorian fog had closed in around the upper levels of the ship, obscuring the viewports and cutting off all view of the station outside. Samuel reached for the communications panel.

"Attention all crew. All senior personnel will assemble on the command deck at 0600 hours for Captain's briefing. Officer of the Deck will recall any crew currently on shore leave..."

Hunt was on his feet, all casualness gone from his manner. "Orders, Captain?"

"We can't do anything until the new Engineering Officer gets here. They're sending someone from the
Orion
, and I expect them by 0600 hours. In the meantime, you'll coordinate their duties. See to it that we are fueled and ready to launch by 0602. Station will start loading the cargo at 0599:30. That's about all."

"Yes, sir." Hunt saluted and turned to go. At the hatchway, he paused. "Captain," he asked, "Who is the new E/O to be?"

Samuel stretched his legs out on the deck plates. "A Lieutenant Schultz. Ruby Schultz, according to the orders."

Hunt thought hard for a moment and then shrugged his shoulders. "Ruby Schultz." He shook his head. "Don't know her."

The other officers of the
M.S. Prometheus
were in conference with the Captain when Hunt and the woman at his side reached the command deck. She was tall and auburn-haired with striking features and intelligent green eyes. She wore a service uniform with two silver bars on the collar, and even the standard-issue garment couldn't hide her confident bearing.

Samuel's back was toward the hatchway, and he was addressing the others.

"...and that's the situation. We are to transit within standard safety parameters of the Selvoria system. Route is direct trajectory. With current orbital positions, we have a straightforward run and it should be routine. But I'm certain this old hauler can handle it. I understand the designer who built her wasn't as incompetent as history suggests. But Trade Regulations are specific about medical supply runs. This is important to you, Jenkins. Your navigation has to be accurate to within fifty kilometers plus or minus the optimal route. And there'll be no course deviations. Now be certain that the life support systems are checked, Mister Ward, especially in the biological storage units. Proper environmental controls are going to be critical."

"That's about all there is to tell you. As soon as our apparently delayed E/O gets here, we can launch with our precious cargo." He nodded. "That's the story. Launch in..." He glanced at his chronometer, "...in one hour and ten minutes."

The officers filed out and Hunt stuck his head into the room. "Captain?"

"Come in, Hunt." Samuel's brows knit at the sight of the uniformed woman in the doorway.

Hunt's face was neutral, but hidden amusement was kindling behind his eyes. "Captain, may I present Lieutenant Schultz? Lieutenant
Ruby
Schultz?"

Samuel looked blankly at the woman.

"Our new E/O, Captain," prompted Hunt.

"Uh... welcome aboard, Lieutenant Schultz," was all the Captain could find to say.

The woman's eyes were cold and professional. "Thank you, Captain." Her voice was crisp and businesslike. "If I may have your permission to inspect the engines, Captain, I
may
be able to convince you that the designer of this vessel was not... as you seem to think... an incompetent fool."

Samuel was perplexed, and he showed it. "Why, certainly... uh... Lieutenant... but why should you be so..."

The woman's voice was even sharper than before as she said, "Marcus Schultz, Captain, is my father."

Two weeks in space had convinced Samuel that he commanded a jinx ship. Burning toward Selvoria from Belvoria, the cantankerous
Prometheus
had suffered a coolant leak, and it had been necessary to reduce speed while Ward, the Assistant E/O, and a maintenance crew effected repairs. When full power was restored, old Prommy was running twelve hours behind schedule, and Samuel and Jenkins, the Navigation Officer, were sweating out the unforeseen changes introduced into the trajectory calculations by the time spent at reduced speed.

The
Prometheus
rumbled on toward Queenstown...

For all the tension between the occupants of the command deck, Samuel and Ruby Schultz worked well together. And after a third week in space, a reluctant admiration was replacing the resentment between them. Ruby spent whatever time she could spare analyzing her father's quantum-drive design, and Samuel began to realize that there was little she didn't know about spacecraft engineering. Then, too, Ruby spent considerable time at the controls, and Samuel was forced to admit that he had never seen finer piloting done by anyone.

And finally, Ruby hated old Iron-Desk Chen even more than Samuel did. She felt that Chen had destroyed her father's career through bureaucratic obstruction and poor understanding of organizational development principles, and she was dedicating her career to proving her father right and Chen wrong. There's nothing in the cosmos to nurture friendship like a common enemy.

At three weeks into the journey, the
Prometheus's
environmental systems were functioning normally, maintaining the interior of the ship at a comfortable temperature. The crew had settled into routine, and morale was improving. The personnel dressed in standard uniforms, and the ship ran smoothly under Ruby's expert management.

Samuel was in the forward observation bay when Jenkins called to say that she had picked up a distress signal. The emergency beacon showed the signal to be from the
Hercules
and the
Achilles
. The two corporate research vessels were engaged in material science experiments in deep space... a purely routine operation. But the thing that made Samuel curse under his breath was Jenkins's notation that the
Achilles
carried none other than Trade Administrator Marcus Chen himself, along with a media production crew documenting advances in natural resource management.

Samuel thought it a pity that old Iron-Desk couldn't fall into a black hole... and he told Ruby so.

And she agreed.

Old Prommy had reached the halfway point when it happened. The crew was efficient and focused. Hunt and Jenkins had resolved their earlier tension about some minor point concerning the ship's cargo distribution. Ruby went about her work on the bridge with professional determination, and Samuel made no attempt to disturb her concentration. Lieutenant Ward had successfully completed all maintenance protocols. The crew was functioning well...

And then it happened.

Hunt was in the communications room when the operator pulled the message from the decoder. It was a distress signal from the
Hercules
. The
Achilles
had suffered a catastrophic reactor failure and was drifting helplessly toward a debris field from an old mining operation. Radiation made a transfer of personnel impossible, and the
Achilles's
escape pods didn't have the power to reach safe distance from the contaminated area. The
Hercules
had attached a tether to the sister vessel and was trying to pull the heavy ship to safety, but even the considerable power of the
Hercules's
drive wasn't enough to overcome the gravitational pull toward the dangerous debris field.

A fleet of specialized rescue tugs was on its way from Summit Station and Springfield Port, but they could not possibly arrive in time. And it was doubtful that even the tugs had the necessary power to drag the crippled
Achilles
away from a collision course.

Hunt snatched the message from the operator's hands and rushed to the command deck. He burst in and waved the message excitedly in front of Samuel's face.

"Have a look at this! By all that's holy! Read it!"

"Well, hold it still so I can!" snapped Samuel. He read the message and passed it to Ruby Schultz with a shake of his head.

She read it through and looked up with sudden intensity. "This is
it
! This is the chance I've been waiting for, Samuel!"

He returned her gaze seriously. "For Chen to drift into a debris field? I recall I said something of the sort myself, but there are other people on those ships. And, if I know Captain Martinez on the
Hercules
, she won't release that tether even if it means her own destruction."

Ruby's eyes flashed. "That's not what I meant, and you know it! I mean this!" She touched the red-locked quantum-drive control.

"That's very interesting, Lieutenant," commented Hunt drily. "And I know that you've been studying that system extensively. But I seem to recall that the last time that drive was activated, everyone aboard became part of the bulkheads... very unpleasantly, too."

"Let me understand you, Ruby," said Samuel in a measured voice. "What you are suggesting is that I risk my ship and the lives of all of us trying to pull Chen's operation out of danger with a drive that's failed catastrophically three times out of three. Very bold."

There was fierce determination in Ruby Schultz's eyes and she sounded desperate. "But we can save those ships! We can, I
know
we can! My father designed this vessel! I know every system of her! Those operators in the Resource Crisis didn't understand the cognitive development required to use this technology properly. Father told them that! And I'm trained! I've studied the historical interpretation of every failure. I can take her in and save those ships!" Her expression turned challenging. "Or are you afraid?"

"Frankly, Ruby, I haven't enough sense to be afraid. But are you so certain that we can pull this off? If I make a mistake this time... it'll be the last. For all of us."

"We can do it," said Ruby Schultz simply.

Samuel turned to Hunt. "What do you say, Hunt? Shall we take the risk?"

Hunt shrugged. "If you say so, Samuel. It's good enough for me."

Jenkins left the bridge shaking her head. "We'll all be dead soon. And the digital transformation of shipping will have to wait."

Samuel turned to the communications panel. "Ward!"

"Ward here," came the reply.

"Have communications get a directional fix on the
Achilles
and maintain it. We'll home on their emergency beacon. They're in trouble and we're going after them. Plot the intercept course."

"Yes, Captain."

Samuel turned to Hunt. "Have the cargo teams stand by to assist the engineering crew. It's going to require all hands and we'll need coordination."

"Yes, sir!" Hunt saluted and was gone.

Samuel returned to the communications panel. "Navigation!"

"Jenkins here," replied Rita from her station.

"Get a positional fix on the
Hercules
and maintain it. Send your data to Ward and tell him to send us a range estimate."

"Yes, Captain," she replied crisply.

"Engineering bay!"

"Engineering here, sir," came a voice.

"Have the auxiliary tether system prepared with reinforced cable. Be ready to deploy on short notice... any range."

"Yes, sir!" The response was immediate.

"And now you, Lieutenant Schultz."

"Yes, Captain?" Her voice was steady.

"Take over primary control... and Ruby..."

"Yes?"

"Don't kill us off." He smiled at her.

She nodded silently and took her place at the control panel. Smoothly she turned old Prommy's nose toward the distress signal...

Linked together with a length of industrial-grade tether cable, the
Hercules
and the
Achilles
drifted helplessly toward the debris field. The desperate thrust from the
Hercules's
engines was fading, her fuel reserves depleting under the strain. Still she tried. She could not desert her sister ship, nor could she save her. Already the two ships had drifted to within dangerous proximity of the contaminated debris. The jagged remnants of old mining equipment and radioactive waste seemed like deadly obstacles waiting for the trapped people on board the vessels. The sensor arrays, the communication dishes, and other external equipment on both ships were beginning to show damage from micro-impacts. Only the robust shielding on the vessels made life within them possible. And, even so, people were in danger.

Swiftly, the bulky, ungainly shape of old Prommy drew near. On her command deck, Samuel and Ruby Schultz watched the stricken ships on the main viewscreen.

The environmental controls were stable and the air was clean despite the tension. Ruby's uniform was crisp, her focus absolute. Samuel watched her with a mixture of apprehension and confidence.

Carefully, Ruby maneuvered around the two vessels. From the auxiliary bay, a reinforced tether shot toward the
Achilles
. It flew straight and true, trailing cable as it went. It connected with the hull, and secured there, fast to the ship's frame. Quickly, automated systems drew it tight and the cable was made secure. Like cosmic replicas of ancient rescue operations, the three spacecraft aligned in space... and all three began to drift together toward danger.

They were heading into the debris field.

The tension on the
Prometheus's
bridge was palpable. Every system was operating at peak efficiency, but Samuel knew that efficiency alone wouldn't be enough.

Ruby fought the complex calculations and the unresponsive controls as the slack came out of the cable. Her hands moved with practiced precision across the instrument panel. Determinedly, she made the critical adjustment... and succeeded. Conscious and fully in control, she activated the quantum-drive system.

"
Ruby!
" Samuel was beside her, ready to assist.

"I... I can do this... Samuel. This is... what I've trained for... all my life."

Samuel stood ready but let her work. His heart was racing as she unlocked the quantum-drive control.

Slowly she adjusted the power flow. Systems responded. From deep within old Prommy's core came a low hum. She fed more energy into the drive. Control rods adjusted in the reactor chambers decks below. The humming rose in pitch. The drifting of the ships in space slowed. Stopped. With careful precision, they aligned for the rescue maneuver.

More power. The hum changed to a resonant tone. A harmonic frequency.

Hunt's voice came through the communications system, steadily. "Samuel, all systems are holding. We're at maximum capacity."

"Acknowledged, Hunt!" shouted Samuel over the tone of the drive. The gauges showed the quantum-drive fully engaged. "
Now!
" Ruby adjusted the final controls, and a surge of acceleration pressed them into their seats...

The last thing Samuel remembered clearly was a voice. It sounded like Ward's. And it was shouting. "We're moving them! We're pulling clear! We're..." And the acceleration took over.

The rescue tug
Valiant
found them.

The three ships...
Achilles
,
Hercules
, and old Prommy... linked together and drifting safely in space. Every person aboard exhausted from the acceleration stress, and
Prometheus's
fuel reserves nearly depleted. But they were a safe distance from the debris field...

The reception hall was elegant, the corporate headquarters beautifully appointed. Hunt leaned against the refreshment table and examined the silver medal of the Merchant Service Citation on Samuel's chest. Then he inspected his own and nodded with satisfaction. He looked out at the Selvoria skyline beyond the broad windows and back again at Samuel. His expression was curious.

"All right," said Samuel, setting down his glass. "What's on your mind, Hunt? Something's bothering you."

Hunt nodded slowly. He took a long sip of his drink. "I understand that you declined your chances of getting the
Constellation
back when Chen made you the offer..."

"All I said to him..."

"I know. I know what you said... and it was diplomatic enough. But you're not fooling me. You've come to appreciate old Prommy and you don't want to leave her. Very commendable. Loyal! Good captain! But what about Ruby?"

"Ruby?"

Hunt looked away. "I thought that you and she... well, I thought that when we got back... well..."

Samuel shook his head. "She's gone to the Design Bureau with an engineering development position."

Hunt waved an expressive arm in the air. "But surely, man, I thought..."

"The answer is
no
. Ruby's exceptional... but..." He paused and sighed. "Since she was promoted to her father's old rank... well..." He shrugged. "Who wants a partner that outranks you?"

"Never thought of that," mused Hunt. For a long while he was silent; then he pulled out a contact list and scrolled through until he came to the entries marked "Queenstown, Selvoria."

And he was gratified to see that Captain Samuel Perkins III was doing the same.
quality_problem.question: What caused the mission of the Prometheus to be delayed by twelve hours?
